Grzegorz Miecugow (22 November 1955 – 26 August 2017) was a Polish television newscaster and journalist. He was born in Kraków, Poland. He was known for presenting the news programs Wiadomości and Fakty TVN. He was also a frequent columnist for Szkło Kontaktowe. Miecugow died of cancer in Warsaw, Poland on 26 August 2017 at the age of 61.

Guadalupe Grande (30 May 1965 – 2 January 2021) was a Spanish poet. She had a degree in social anthropology from the Complutense University of Madrid. She was born in Madrid. She was a literary critic and teacher. She wrote El libro de Lilit in 1995, La llave de la niebla in 2003, and Mapas de cera in 2006. Grande died at the age of 55 due to coronavirus in his hometown of Madrid, Spain, on January 2, 2021.

Gualtiero Marchesi (; 19 March 1930 – 26 December 2017) was an Italian chef. He was thought to be the founder of modern Italian cuisine. He was born in Milan. He then opened his first restaurant on Via Bonvesin de la Riva in Milan. Within a year he earned his first Michelin star, with another following the next year. It took another seven years, but then he eventually won the distinction of a third Michelin star – the first chef in Italy to do so. In 2011, Marchesi became the first celebrity chef to design two hamburgers and a dessert for McDonald's. In May 2017, Marchesi and Director Maurizio Gigola presented the Documentary "Marchesi: The Great Italian" at the Cannes Film Festival. Marchesi died in Rome on 26 December 2017 of cardiac arrest at the age of 87.

Guan Daosheng, also called Guan Zhongji or Lady Zhongji (her courtesy name) (; 字仲姬；1262–1319), was a Chinese painter and poet. She wrote and drew during the early Yuan dynasty. She is said to be "the most famous female painter and calligrapher in the Chinese history." She was also a popular poet from the Yuan dynasty.

Gucci, is an Italian fashion house (fashion design company). It was started by Guccio Gucci (1881 – 1953) in Florence in 1909. Gucci is one of the most famous, successful, and easily recognizable fashion brands in the world. Gucci is now owned by the French conglomerate company, Kering. BusinessWeek magazine says that Gucci made more than US$7 billion in 2006, and was 46th in the magazine's yearly "Top 100 Brands". Gucci is the second biggest selling fashion brand after LVMH. It is the biggest selling Italian brand in the world. It has about 425 shops around the world. Its products are also sold by franchisees and department stores. Gucci was started in 1906 by Guccio Gucci. In 1938, Gucci grew bigger, and a small shop opened in Rome. Guccio Gucci designed many of the company's famous clothes. In 1947, Gucci made the bamboo-handle handbag, which is still used. In the 1950s, Gucci also made the striped webbing (a type of material), and the suede and metal moccasin shoes. Guccio Gucci's wife, Aida Calvelli had a large family, with six children, but only their four sons (Vasco, Aldo, Ugo, and Rodolfo) helped lead the company. After Guccio's death in 1953, Aldo helped lead the company to being a major fashion shop in more countries. He opened the company’s first small shops in London, Paris, and New York. Arguments about inheritances, stock holdings, and day-to-day operations of the shops often divided the family, and caused alliances to be made. Gucci grew in other countries. Gucci decided to grow a lot in East Asia in the late 1960s. He opened shops in Hong Kong (China), Tokyo (Japan), and Korea. At that time, the company also made its famous GG logo (Guccio Gucci's initials), and the Flora silk scarf (worn most notably by Hollywood actress Grace Kelly), and the "Jackie O shoulder" bag, which was made famous by Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis, the widow of U.S. President John F. Kennedy. Gucci was one of the biggest luxury clothes companies in the world until the late 1970s, when some bad business decisions and family arguments almost made the company bankrupt. At the time, the brothers Aldo and Rodolfo controlled equal 50% shares of the company. In 1979, Aldo made the 'Gucci Accessories Collection', or 'GAC', which was meant to increase sales for the Gucci Parfums sector, which his sons controlled. GAC sold small accessories, such as cosmetic bags, lighters, and pens, which were cheaper than the other items in the company’s accessories catalogue. Aldo gave control of Parfums to his son Roberto in an effort to weaken Rodolfo’s control of the overall operations of the company. Aldo Gucci's expansion into new markets included an agreement with American Motors Corporation (AMC). In 1972 the compact AMC Hornet "Sportabout" was one of the first American cars to be offered with a luxury trim package created by a famous fashion designer. The Gucci cars had striped green, red, and buff material inside, as well as the Gucci's logos and outside color selections. The "Gucci Accessories Collection" was popular, but it brought the Gucci strength down. After a few years, the "Parfums section" started to sell better than the "Accessories section". The newly-made wholesaling business brought the once-exclusive brand to over a thousand stores in the United States alone with the GAC line. This damaged the brand’s standing with fashionable customers. "In the 1960s and 1970s," writes Vanity Fair editor Graydon Carter, "Gucci had been at the pinnacle of chic, thanks to icons such as Audrey Hepburn, Grace Kelly, and Jacqueline Onassis. But by the 1980s, Gucci had lost its appeal, becoming a tacky airport brand."

Gudrun Pausewang (3 March 1928 – 23 January 2020) was a German writer for children and teens. She was also known in science fiction for Young-Adult novels such as The Last Children of Schewenborn. She was born in Mladkov, Czech Republic and was a teacher and emptied at German Schools in Chile and Venezuela, but above all at the German School of Barranquilla in Colombia; and traveled to North, Central and South America, including the Amazon Basin, Tierra del Fuego, Peru, Bolivia and Mexico. She died at the age of 91 near Bamberg in Germany. In 1988, her novel Die Wolke (The Cloud) won the Deutscher Jugendliteraturpreis ("German Youth Literature Prize"), the Kurd-Laßwitz-Preis ("Kurd Lasswitz Prize"), and the Deutscher Science Fiction Preis ("German Science Fiction Prize") for Best Novel. Her sister was writer and sociologist Freya Pausewang.

Gudrun Zapf-von Hesse (January 2, 1918 – December 13, 2019) was a German type designer, calligrapher and book-binder. She was the 1991 winner of the Frederic W. Goudy Award. She also designed several fonts. She was born in Schwerin, Germany. In her early years, she worked with Rudolf Koch and Edward Johnston. From 1946 to 1954, Von Hesse taught lettering at the Städelschule in Frankfurt. She was hired by the Stempel foundry in Frankfurt to design typefaces, and went on to a successful career as a typographer with Stempel. In 2001, she was recognized with a Lifetime Achievement Award from the Friends of Calligraphy. She turned 100 in January 2018. From 1951 until his death in 2015, she was married to Hermann Zapf. They had one son Christian, who died in 2012. She lived in Darmstadt, Germany. She died on December 13, 2019 at the age of 101. Hesse-Antiqua (2018, Monotype, with Ferdinand Ulrich)

Gudrun Margarete Elfriede Emma Anna Burwitz (née Himmler, 8 August 1929 – 24 May 2018) was a German Nazi supporter and the daughter of Margarete Himmler and Heinrich Himmler. She was born in Munich. Burwitz was arrested and made to testify at the Nuremberg trials. She fought to defend her father’s reputation and became closely involved in Neo-Nazi groups that give support to ex-members of the SS. Burwitz died on 24 May 2018 at her home near Munich, aged 88. Her death was announced a month later.
Guccio Gucci (26 March 1881 – 2 January 1953) was an Italian-British businessman and fashion designer. He is most known for being the founder of the fashion house of Gucci.

Guem, stage name of Abdelmajid Guemguem (9 March 1947 – 22 January 2021) was an Algerian percussionist. He composed Le Serpent, re-recorded in 1996 for the program on France 2. In 2011, he composed Mon Paris. Guem died on 22 January 2021 in Paris, aged 73.

Guglielmo Marconi (25 April 1874 20 July 1937) was an Italian inventor and electrical engineer. He was a pioneer of long-distance radio transmission. which he used to build up a radio telegraph system. Marconi is often named as the inventor of radio. He shared the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics with Karl Ferdinand Braun. Much of Marconi's work in radio transmission was built on previous experimentation, and work by others. When he was twenty years old, based on the experiments of Hertz, Popov, Lodge, Bose, and Tesla, Marconi began his own experiments. As an entrepreneur, businessman, and founder of The Wireless Telegraph & Signal Company in Britain in 1897, Marconi became wealthy in the business of radio, mainly for ships at sea. In 1924, he was ennobled as Marchese Marconi. Back in Italy, he went on to become a member of the Grand Council of Fascism.

Guido (von) List (born Karl Anton List; 5 October 1848 in Vienna – 17 May 1919 in Berlin) was an Austrian writer. His works were influenced very much by ideas of race. He was influenced by Arthur de Gobineau, Helena Petrovna Blavatsky, and others. He believed there was a global jewish conspiracy. He thought that the conspiracy threatened those he believed to be the Aryan race. He also believed that runes had magic power. His beliefs were not unpopular in Western Europe in the 19th century. He was an occultist. A contemporary of his was Houston Steward Chamberlain. Chambelain lived at the same time as he did. One of his successors was Jörg Lanz von Liebenfels. He is attributed with suggesting the swastika as the symbol for all “anti-Semitic” organizations. This symbol was later introduced in the Nazi flag inside a white circle with a red background.

Guido Cavalcanti (1259 – August 1300) was an Italian poet from Florence. He was the best friend of Dante Alighieri as well as an influence on his thinking. Cavalcanti is one of the most important poets of Dolce stil novo, and he is widely regarded as the first major poet of Italian literature. Cavalcanti was born into a noble Guelph family; his father was Cavalcante de Cavalcanti. In 1267 he got married to Bice, daughter of Farinata degli Uberti, leader of the Florentine Ghibellines. In 1284 he became a member of the general council, together with Brunetto Latini and Dino Compagni. On June 24 1300 he was exiled, so he went to Sarzana. On August 19 of the same year he could return in Florence, but he died after a few days, on August 29. Guido Cavalcanti wrote sonnets and ballads. Only fifty two poems by the poet are known today. Hist best works are the canzone Donna mi prega (A lady asks me), the ballad I' prego voi che di dolor parlate (I ask you that speak about suffering) and the sonnet L’anima mia vilment’ è sbigotita (My soul is in distress). Cavalcanti's poems were translated into English by Dante Gabriel Rossetti, Ezra Pound and A.S. Kline.

Guido Gezelle (1 May 1830 – 27 November 1899) was a Roman Catholic priest from Belgium. He was also a writer, translator and poet. Gezelle was born and died in Bruges. He became priest in 1854. Gezelle's parents were Pieter Jan Gezelle and Monica Devrieze. He was an uncle of the Flemish writer Stijn Streuvels. Gezelle is still famous now for his translation of The Song of Hiawatha by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow.

Guido Altarelli (July 12, 1941 - September 30, 2015) was an Italian theoretical physicist. He was born in Rome, Italy. He held positions at New York University (1968–69), the Rockefeller University (New York, 1969–70), l' École Normale Supérieure in Paris (76-77, 81), and Boston University (85-86). 2011 Julius Wess Award for Outstanding Achievements in Elementary Particle and Astroparticle Physics - The Karlsruhe Institute of Technology 2012 J. J. Sakurai Prize for Theoretical Particle Physics - The American Physical Society High Energy and Particle Physics Prize - EPS HEPP Prize, 2015.

Guido Ceronetti (24 August 1927 – 13 September 2018) was an Italian poet, philosopher, novelist, translator, journalist and playwright. He was born in Turin, Italy. In 1970, he founded the Theater of the Sensitive. His works are archived at the Cantonal Library of Lugano. He wrote columns for La Repubblica, La Stampa and Radio Radicale. Emil Cioran dedicated to his book Il silenzio del corpo ("The Silence of the Body") a chapter of the essay Exercices d'admiration (1986). Ceronetti died in Cetona, Italy on 13 September 2018 from bronchopneumonia at the age of 91.

Guido Wilhelmus Imbens (born September 3, 1963) is a Dutch-American economist. He is Professor of Economics at the Stanford Graduate School of Business. He taught at Harvard University, UCLA, and UC Berkeley. He was the editor of Econometrica beginning in 2019. Imbens was awarded half of the 2021 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences with Joshua Angrist "for their works to the analysis of causal relationships", with David Card awarded the other half.

Guillaume Le Vasseur de Beauplan (around 1600-December 6, 1673) was a cartographer, engineer and architect from France. He was in the military in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth army from 1630 until the late 1640's. He was forced to move to Ukraine. He was in the military under Stanisław Koniecpolski for one year in 1637. While in the military he helped rebuild the Kodak Fortress. He also built other fortresses in Bar, Ukraine. He also helped build Brody Castle and other buildings in Kremenchuk, Ukraine. He created the first well described map of Ukraine in 1639. In 1648 he made another map of Ukraine that was very detailed. He moved to Danzig. He made two other very detailed maps and they were engraved by Willem Hondius. He wrote a book called Description d'Ukranie. It was originally named Description des contrés du Royaume de Pologne, when it was first published in 1651. It was published two more times, until 1861. It was the first book to write about Ukraine in great detail. It's still in print today.

Guillaume Faye (; 7 November 1949 – 7 March 2019) was a French journalist and writer. He was born in Angoulême, France. In 1987, Guillaume Faye withdrew from politics. In 1990, he took part in Skyrock radio station as 'Skyman'. He also appeared in Telematin episodes on the France 2 TV channel from 1991 to 1993. He took part in the Rivarol. Faye died of complications from lung cancer on 7 March 2019, aged 69.

Guillaume Gevart (born February 12, 1997) is a French filmmaker. After obtaining his literary baccalaureate at Lycée externat des Enfants-Nantais, he studied cinema at CinéCréatis then in an art school in Nantes. Since he was a child, he has been a fan of films from the 50s to the 90s. He began his career by following internships at Disney Channel. In 2019, he produced and directed his first film entitled Yearning Rose with an approximate budget of 13,000 dollars, a film which has the particularity of having been filmed in 7 days. He then worked as a camera operator on the documentary La légende de Thierry Mauvignier. His work is based on fast-movie, a cinematographic movement which consists of producing a feature film (sequence shot excluded) in less than 10 days with a low budget, prioritizing efficiency over quality. In October 2022, The film is distributed by Amazon Prime Video in USA. In 2023, he directed the medium-length film The Venus Chained produced by Jacob Rothschild and Dylan Besseau, in collaboration with the Mouvement du Nid on Prime Video distributed by Apple TV+ and Tubi. At the end of the year he produced the film Anne Bouillon: Justice pour toutes !. In 2023, his film The Venus Chained wins honorable mention at Student World Impact Film Festival. The same year, he was selected for the prestigious Justice Documentary Festival Paris 2023. He was the youngest director in the selection. In 2024, he directed the documentary Gevart. Born to a doctor father. 2023 Honorable Mention at Student World Impact Film Festival 2023 Official Selection at Justice Documentary Festival Paris

Guillaume Apollinaire (; 26 August 1880 – 9 November 1918) was a French poet, writer, and art critic. His real name was Wilhelm Albert Włodzimierz Apolinary Kostrowicki. He was born in Rome, Italy. His mother came from a Polish family. He did not become a French citizen until 1916. He is seen as one of the most important French poets of the early 20th century. Apollinaire wrote two famous books of poetry. The first was Alcools (1913). Its poems were printed without punctuation, such as commas and full stops. The second was Calligrammes (1918). Some of its poems use words to make pictures on the page. Apollinaire was a close friend of the painter Pablo Picasso. He was also a strong supporter of Cubism, which was then a new style of painting. In 1912, he gave the name Orphism to another art movement. In 1917, he made the word surréalisme, which means "surrealism". Some people who study art history also say that he helped make the word "Cubism" popular. His play Les Mamelles de Tirésias appeared in 1917. He called it a "surrealist drama". Francis Poulenc later made it into an opera, first performed in 1947. Apollinaire fought as a French soldier in the First World War. In March 1916, a piece of an exploding shell went through his helmet and wounded him in the head. He later returned to his busy life as a writer, but he never became fully healthy again. He died in Paris on 9 November 1918. This was two days before the Armistice, which stopped the fighting. He died during the Spanish flu, a serious influenza pandemic that spread around the world in 1918. He was 38 years old. After his death, young writers such as André Breton and Louis Aragon saw Apollinaire as a guide. In 1924, they used his word "surrealism" as the name of their own movement. Today, his work is studied in many schools. Poems such as "Le Pont Mirabeau" and "Zone" are among the best-known poems in the French language. "Guillaume Apollinaire" was a pen name, or a name that a writer uses for his work. The poet made it from his real names. "Guillaume" is the French form of "Wilhelm", his first name. "Apollinaire" was another of his given names. It was also the first name of his Polish grandfather. When he was young, his mother and his friends called him "Wilhelm" or "Kostro". The name "Guillaume Apollinaire" was first printed on 10 August 1901. He used it under an article in a small weekly paper that made fun of people and events. In March 1902, an important Paris magazine called La Revue blanche printed his story "L'Hérésiarque" under the new name. In 1903, he wrote to a young Englishwoman whom he loved. He told her that she could now write to him under the name "Guillaume Apollinaire". The name "Apollinaire" also made people think of the Greek god Apollo, the god of poetry and light. Apollinaire liked this connection very much. Apollinaire was born in Rome at the end of August 1880. His official date of birth was 26 August, but some writers believe that he was born one day earlier. A few days later, a midwife reported his birth at the town hall. A midwife is a woman who helps mothers when they give birth. She used the false name "Guglielmo Alberto Dulcigni" and said that the baby's parents were unknown. The child was baptized at the church of San Vito on 29 September. On 2 November, his mother told a notary that he was her son. A notary is a public officer who records legal facts and prepares official papers. She gave the child her own family name. His full name then became Guglielmo Alberto Wladimiro Alessandro Apollinare de Kostrowitzky. His mother, Angelica de Kostrowitzky, was 22 years old. Her father, Michel Apollinaire Kostrowicki, was a Polish nobleman, and her mother, Julie Floriani, was Italian. The family had left Poland after the failed January Uprising of 1863. At that time, Russia ruled the part of Poland where they had lived. Two of Michel's brothers were sent to Siberia, and the family lost its lands near Navahrudak. Michel moved to Rome. There he became a chamberlain at the court of Pope Pius IX. A chamberlain was an officer who served a ruler or an important religious leader. Angelica grew up in a strict convent school in Rome. French was the language used there every day. However, she was proud and did not like to obey rules. As a young woman, she lived alone among the rich people of Rome. People at the time called her a "kept woman". This meant that rich lovers gave her money and paid for her way of life. Apollinaire never officially knew who his father was. The man most often named as his father is Francesco Flugi d'Aspermont. He was an Italian army officer from an old noble family of Swiss origin. He was about 44 years old when he met Angelica at her first ball. She ran away with him. For several years, they travelled through Italy and southern France, but they never married. Flugi d'Aspermont left the family around 1884 or 1885, when Guillaume was still a young child. Apollinaire probably knew who his father was. One of his friends said that, around 1900, Apollinaire showed him a photograph of an Italian officer and said, "This is my father". However, he never told the public the truth. He sometimes joked that his father was a cardinal or even the Pope. The missing father became an important subject in his poetry. His poems often speak about people who do not know where they belong and about travellers who move from one place to another. In June 1882, Angelica had another son, Albert. His birth was also reported under a false name. Writers do not agree about whether Albert and Guillaume had the same father. Guillaume and Albert remained close throughout their lives. Albert later worked in a bank and moved to Mexico. Apollinaire's first picture-poem, "Lettre-Océan" (1914), was written as a letter to his brother far away. In March 1887, Angelica moved with her two sons to Monaco, a small country beside France on the Mediterranean Sea. She now called herself "Olga" and spent much of her time at the casino in Monte Carlo. In October of the same year, Wilhelm entered the Collège Saint-Charles. It was a Catholic boarding school, where pupils lived as well as studied. Wilhelm was a very good pupil. He won many school prizes and was a deeply religious child. For a time, he even thought about becoming a priest. At Saint-Charles, he made friends who remained close to him for the rest of his life. They included René Dupuy, who later became a writer under the name René Dalize, and Louis de Gonzague Frick, who later became a poet. In 1889, his mother took the two boys on a short visit to Paris. They saw the World's Fair and the new Eiffel Tower. The Collège Saint-Charles closed in 1895. In 1896, Wilhelm entered the Collège Stanislas in Cannes. In May, the school sent him away because he had brought in a forbidden book. In October 1896, he entered the lycée, or high school, in Nice. There he made another lifelong friend, Ange Toussaint Luca. Wilhelm read a very large number of books. He read ancient Greek and Latin writers and the great French novels. He also read forbidden books, old stories and legends, and anarchist newspapers. Anarchists were against government and political authority. In July 1897, he passed the written part of the baccalauréat, the French examination taken at the end of high school. However, he never received the full diploma and left school without it. He never studied at a university. Even so, his friends later said that he seemed to know everything. He educated himself by reading in libraries. This wide and unusual knowledge appears throughout his poetry. In 1899, Angelica left Monaco with her two sons and her companion, Jules Weil, a businessman whom she had known since her years in Monaco. After short stays in Aix-les-Bains and Lyon, they arrived in Paris in April. In the middle of July, Angelica left the two boys in Stavelot, a small town in the Walloon part of Belgium, among the Ardennes hills. She went to try her luck at the casino in nearby Spa. She was not allowed into the gaming rooms, and she and Weil soon moved on to Ostend, leaving the boys behind. Wilhelm spent a happy summer in Stavelot. He walked across the high moors called the Fagnes, listened to the Walloon language spoken by the villagers, and fell in love with Maria Dubois, the daughter of a café owner. He wrote his first real love poems for her. He also learned enough Walloon to use it in his writing for many years. It gave him material for a short story called "Que vlo-ve ?", which means "What do you want?" in Walloon. He also used it in a chapter of Le Poète assassiné and in a war poem written in 1914. However, the boys soon had no money left. On 5 October 1899, following their mother's orders, they quietly left their guesthouse at dawn without paying the bill. They then took the train back to Paris. The angry owner of the guesthouse went to the police, but the case was closed without punishment in January 1900. This small and shameful event stayed in Apollinaire's memory. Throughout his life, he remained a poor man among rich friends, a foreigner without proper papers, and someone who could be forced to leave at any time. In Paris, he was officially recorded as a foreigner of Russian nationality under the name "Guillaume Kostrowitzky". This paper was his only identity document until 1916. The family settled in Paris, and Wilhelm began looking for work. Because he was a foreigner and did not have a diploma, he could not work in the French public administration. He took several small jobs. In the spring of 1900, he secretly wrote parts of a newspaper serial called Que faire ? ("What to Do?"). A serial is a story published in separate parts. It appeared in the daily newspaper Le Matin under the name of another man, the lawyer Henry Esnard. He earned a diploma in shorthand, a system used for writing very quickly. From July 1900, he worked as a secretary in a small financial office. In his free time, he read rare books at the Bibliothèque Mazarine, one of the oldest libraries in Paris. There he met the scholar Léon Cahun. Cahun introduced him to medieval stories and languages from distant countries. He also introduced him to his nephew, the writer Marcel Schwob. In 1900, Wilhelm fell in love with Linda Molina da Silva, the young sister of a friend. He sent her poems, but she did not answer them. In May 1901, Apollinaire's life changed. A rich woman, the Viscountess Elinor de Milhau, employed him as the private teacher of her nine-year-old daughter, Gabrielle. In August 1901, the whole household travelled by car to Germany. They went to the Rhineland, the area around the river Rhine. They first lived near Honnef and later in a country house called "Neu-Glück", near Oberpleis. Apollinaire spent a full year discovering German life. He saw vineyards, ruined castles above the river, forests of fir trees, village festivals, and Christmas markets. He also learned the old legends of the Lorelei. During the first months of 1902, the viscountess took the household on a long journey through Germany. Apollinaire saw the carnival in Cologne and visited Berlin, Dresden, and Munich. In March, he travelled alone to Prague and Vienna. Prague made a particularly strong impression on him. He later used the city in one of his best short stories, "Le Passant de Prague" ("The Wanderer of Prague"). The story is based on the legend of the Wandering Jew. This year in Germany gave him the "Rhénanes", or "Rhineland poems". They form one of the most beautiful groups of poems in Alcools. In poems such as "Nuit rhénane", "Mai", and "La Loreley", German folk songs, drinking songs, and river legends are mixed with the poet's own sadness. In September 1901, Apollinaire also published his first poems. They appeared in a small Paris magazine called La Grande France. One of them later became the poem called "Clair de lune" in Alcools. While he was in Germany, Apollinaire fell deeply in love. The governess in the Milhau household was Annie Playden, a young Englishwoman from south London. A governess was a woman employed to teach and care for children. Annie was blonde, pretty, and shy. She came from a very strict religious family. At first, she seemed to return Apollinaire's love. Later, she became frightened by the strength of his feelings and moved away from him. In August 1902, Apollinaire left his job and returned to Paris. Annie's cold behaviour had deeply hurt him. However, he did not give up. In November 1903, he travelled to London and tried to win her back. He returned again in May 1904. He found Landor Road, the grey street of small brick houses where Annie's family lived. He walked with her through the foggy streets of London. When he returned to Paris at the end of May, he was still hopeful. The visit had not ended in a complete break. At the beginning of 1905, however, Annie left Europe for the United States. She later said that one reason for leaving was to escape from Apollinaire. He then understood that he had lost her. Annie worked in the United States as a governess and never read Apollinaire's books. Researchers found her in America only in the 1950s. They told her, to her great surprise, that she had become one of the most famous loved women in French poetry. The memory of Annie appears throughout Alcools. She is the distant woman in "La Chanson du mal-aimé" ("The Song of the Badly-Loved"). This long poem tells of a young man who follows a woman through London but is refused by her. Apollinaire wrote most of the poem in 1903. It was not published until 1 May 1909, in the Mercure de France. Annie is also the young woman who leaves her country in "L'Émigrant de Landor Road". She appears again in the short and sad poem "Annie", which is set in Texas. Pascal Pia, one of Apollinaire's biographers, wrote that Annie Playden's shadow lies over a whole part of Alcools. Through this experience, Apollinaire learned an idea that became central to his poetry: for him, love would almost always be a love that had been lost. Apollinaire returned to Paris in August 1902. He lived with his mother again and looked for work. He wrote for a small weekly newspaper about European affairs called L'Européen. In June 1903, he began working as a clerk in a bank. He later worked in several other banks and financial offices until 1907. During the day, he copied numbers. At night, he wrote. La Revue blanche, an important literary magazine, published his first short stories. These were strange and learned tales about heretics, false gods, and wandering souls. Heretics are people who reject the official teachings of a religion. For the first time, he signed these works with the name "Guillaume Apollinaire". In 1903, he began attending the evening meetings of the magazine La Plume. Many young poets of Paris met there. He became friends with the poet André Salmon, with Alfred Jarry, the wild writer of Ubu Roi, and with Jean Mollet. Mollet later became his loyal, unpaid secretary. In November 1903, Apollinaire started a small magazine with Salmon, Mollet, and the poet Nicolas Deniker. It was called Le Festin d'Ésope, or "Aesop's Feast". Only nine issues appeared. In this magazine, Apollinaire published his first long prose work one chapter at a time. It was called L'Enchanteur pourrissant, or "The Rotting Enchanter". It is a dream-like dialogue about the wizard Merlin, who is buried alive by the fairy who loves him. Even this very small magazine taught Apollinaire an important lesson. Modern poetry needed its own magazines and other places where it could appear freely, away from the large newspapers that were controlled by business. One evening in February 1905, Apollinaire was waiting for the last train home in a bar near the Saint-Lazare railway station. Jean Mollet brought a young Spanish painter to his table. The painter was almost unknown and very poor. His name was Pablo Picasso. Writers about their lives often describe this meeting as an important turning point for both men. The next day, Picasso introduced Apollinaire to his closest friend, the poet Max Jacob. The three men understood one another immediately. Picasso lived on the hill of Montmartre in a strange wooden building filled with artists' studios. Max Jacob called it the "Bateau-Lavoir", or "washing-boat", because it looked like the boats on the river Seine where women washed clothes. Apollinaire returned to Montmartre again and again. He saw the sad blue pictures of Picasso's "blue period" and the circus performers of his "rose period". In the spring of 1905, Apollinaire wrote his first two articles about Picasso. One appeared in La Revue immoraliste, a small magazine that he had recently started with Mollet and Salmon. The other appeared in La Plume. These were among the first important articles written about Picasso. Apollinaire had found another kind of work: he would explain modern painting to the public. A famous group of friends grew around Picasso and Apollinaire. It became known as the "bande à Picasso", or "Picasso's gang". Its members included Max Jacob, André Salmon, and later many other artists and writers. They were poor, humorous, and hard-working. They were also completely sure that they were changing art forever. In April 1907, when he was twenty-six years old, Apollinaire finally left his mother's home. He rented his first flat near Montmartre. One month later, Picasso returned from the small shop of the art dealer Clovis Sagot. With a very serious expression, he told Apollinaire that he had found a future wife for him there. Apollinaire quickly went to the shop and met the young painter Marie Laurencin. She was twenty-three years old, clever, gifted, and often ironic. She painted soft grey-and-pink pictures of young women, deer, and flowers. Apollinaire and Marie loved one another for five difficult years. They argued, separated, and then came together again. Apollinaire's mother believed that Marie was not rich enough for her son. After 1911, Marie's mother no longer wanted Apollinaire to visit her daughter. By the end of 1911, their love was slowly ending, and Apollinaire knew it. This feeling helped him write "Le Pont Mirabeau", or "The Mirabeau Bridge". The poem was published in February 1912 and is perhaps his best-loved poem. In it, the river Seine flows under a bridge in Paris and carries love away, while the poet remains behind. In June 1912, after another serious quarrel, Marie left Apollinaire for the last time. Their friends tried to bring them together again, but they failed. Apollinaire became deeply depressed, and this sadness lasted throughout the summer. He left Auteuil, the area where he and Marie had lived near one another. At the end of the year, he rented a flat at 202 boulevard Saint-Germain. It remained his home for the rest of his life. In June 1914, Marie married the German painter Otto von Wätjen. A few weeks later, the war made France and Germany enemy countries. From 1910, Apollinaire earned his living as a journalist. He wrote a daily art column for the newspaper L'Intransigeant. From 1911, he also wrote a famous column of news and stories called "La Vie anecdotique" for the Mercure de France. He reviewed almost every important art exhibition in Paris. Most critics laughed at the new painters, but Apollinaire defended them. These artists included Henri Matisse, André Derain, Georges Braque, Robert Delaunay, Marcel Duchamp, the young Marc Chagall, the dream-like painter Giorgio de Chirico, and above all Picasso and the Cubists. His support for the newest art had a cost. In March 1914, the director of L'Intransigeant became tired of Apollinaire's constant praise for modern painters and took the art column away from him. Apollinaire then moved to another newspaper, Paris-Journal. He also admired painters whom almost nobody else respected. The old painter Henri Rousseau was known as "le Douanier", or "the customs officer". He painted jungles and dreams in a simple, childlike style. Official critics laughed at him, but Apollinaire understood his importance. Rousseau painted a large double portrait of Apollinaire and Marie Laurencin called The Muse Inspiring the Poet in 1909. To make the portrait accurate, he measured Apollinaire's face and body with a ruler. In November 1908, Picasso organized a famous banquet in Rousseau's honour at the Bateau-Lavoir. A banquet is a large formal meal. Poets and painters crowded into the studio. They sang songs in Rousseau's honour, and the old painter sat in the place of honour under paper lanterns. The year 1908 was an important turning point for Apollinaire. In May, he wrote to his old school friend Toussaint Luca and described his aim in one sentence. He wanted "un lyrisme neuf et humaniste à la fois": a form of poetry that was completely new but still deeply human. Within a few months, he published a strange prose poem called "Onirocritique", or "Dream-criticism". In it, an enchanter walks through a dream world where flames become flowers. He also gave a public talk about young poets. He wrote two introductions about modern painting, in which the flame became a symbol of art. He also published two long poems that he always considered among his deepest works: "Le Brasier", or "The Brazier", and "Les Fiançailles", or "The Betrothal". In these poems, the poet throws his old self into the fire. Like the Phoenix, the legendary bird that burns and is then born again, he returns from the flames with new powers. Scholars often see 1908 as the passage between the young Apollinaire, who was still close to Symbolism, and the fully modern poet. One figure appears behind all these works: the enchanter. Since his summer in Stavelot in 1899, Apollinaire had continued to write and rewrite his book about Merlin, L'Enchanteur pourrissant. When the book finally appeared in 1909, "Onirocritique" became its final chapter. A short animal poem from the same year shows his fear of time passing. He wrote: Dieu ! Je vais avoir vingt-huit ans / Et mal vécus, à mon envie ("God! I am going to be twenty-eight, and I have not lived as well as I wished"). That summer, while spending a holiday on the coast of the North Sea, he made an important decision. He would leave his bank job and earn his living only through writing. Apollinaire's first books appeared slowly and in very small numbers. They were also beautiful objects made together with artists. L'Enchanteur pourrissant, his book about Merlin, was printed in November 1909. The young art dealer Daniel-Henry Kahnweiler published only about one hundred copies. The book included dark woodcuts by André Derain. Woodcuts are pictures made from designs cut into wood. The work is often described as one of the first important modern "painters' books", in which writing and art are designed together. L'Hérésiarque et Cie, or "The Heresiarch and Co.", appeared in October 1910. It brought together twenty-three of Apollinaire's best short stories. They tell of false prophets, miracles, crimes, and wandering people, often with dark humour. In December 1910, the book received several votes for the Prix Goncourt, the most famous French prize for literature. The prize was finally given to Louis Pergaud. Apollinaire believed for the rest of his life that the prize had been unfairly taken from him. Le Bestiaire ou Cortège d'Orphée, or "The Bestiary, or Procession of Orpheus", appeared in March 1911. It is a group of very short poems about animals, usually only four to six lines long. The animals include the dromedary, the mouse, the carp, and the dove. A woodcut by Raoul Dufy appeared beside each poem. Only 120 copies were printed. Behind its jokes about animals, the small book is really about Orpheus, the first poet of Greek legend, and about poetry itself. Apollinaire also enjoyed literary jokes. In 1909, he invented a young woman poet called "Louise Lalanne". He wrote poems and articles under her name for the magazine Les Marges. Critics praised this new and fresh female voice. Some of the poems were actually written by Marie Laurencin. Apollinaire also wrote many works simply to earn money, both under his own name and under false names. These included introductions to old erotic books, popular novels, and hundreds of newspaper articles. He knew both the popular and the serious sides of literature. He later used material from both worlds in his poetry. In August 1911, the Mona Lisa, the most famous painting in the world, was stolen from the Louvre museum in Paris. Newspapers wrote about the theft every day, and the affair had serious effects on Apollinaire's life. The story behind it was unusual. In 1907, a charming but dishonest young Belgian called Géry Pieret had secretly stolen two small ancient Iberian stone statues from the Louvre. He sold them to Picasso. Pieret had once worked as Apollinaire's secretary. Picasso kept the statues. Some art historians believe that they helped him move toward Cubism. In 1911, Pieret returned to Paris and stole another statue. After the Mona Lisa disappeared, he sold this statue to a newspaper. He wanted to show how badly the Louvre protected its works of art. The police began looking for the newspaper's unknown thief. Apollinaire became frightened and helped Pieret leave France by train. Then Apollinaire and a very frightened Picasso took the two earlier statues to the newspaper so that they could be secretly returned to the museum. It was already too late. On 7 September 1911, the police arrested Apollinaire at his home. A judge accused him of helping the thieves and sent him to the Santé prison in Paris. For the newspapers, it was an exciting story: a foreign poet, known as a leader of strange modern art, was connected with the theft of the Mona Lisa. Picasso was questioned by the judge. At first, he denied everything. According to some accounts, he even denied that Apollinaire was his friend. Apollinaire spent five days and nights in a cell at the Santé prison. He was released on 12 September. In January 1912, the case against him was completely dropped. The real thief of the Mona Lisa was an Italian worker called Vincenzo Peruggia. He was caught only in 1913, and the painting was returned to the Louvre. The affair left deep emotional wounds. Apollinaire was still a foreigner and feared that France would force him to leave. He wanted very much to become a French citizen. Some newspapers attacked him with hateful words about his foreign birth. While in prison, he wrote a group of short and painful poems called "À la Santé", or "At the Santé". He later included them in Alcools. In these poems, the prisoner no longer has a name. He is only a number: "le quinze de la Onzième", or "number fifteen of the eleventh division". Even the sky is described as "blue like a chain": (In a pit like a bear / Every morning I walk round and round) The short series recalls the prison poems that Paul Verlaine had written about forty years earlier. Even the critic who later attacked Alcools most strongly admitted that these poems were deeply moving. They had been written at a moment when Apollinaire had forgotten all literary art and felt only pain. In February 1912, Apollinaire and four friends founded a new magazine called Les Soirées de Paris, or "Paris Evenings". The founders included the writer André Billy and René Dalize, Apollinaire's old school friend from Monaco. "Le Pont Mirabeau" appeared in the first issue. In November 1913, after the magazine had stopped for a time, it began again with money from the painter Serge Férat and the baroness Hélène d'Oettingen. Apollinaire now directed the magazine himself and made it the main place for his ideas. The magazine published the new poets. It was also one of the first magazines anywhere to print pictures of Cubist paintings. Many readers cancelled their subscriptions because they disliked the new art. Apollinaire continued without changing direction. These were years of constant movement and invention. In October 1912, Apollinaire stayed in the Jura hills with the painter Francis Picabia and Marcel Duchamp. He read them his newest poem, "Zone". In a public talk during the same month, he announced a new form of Cubism. He called it "Orphism", after Orpheus. It was a kind of painting based on pure colour and light. For Apollinaire, its main artist was Robert Delaunay. In January 1913, he travelled to Berlin to speak at an exhibition of Delaunay's work. For the exhibition, he wrote "Les Fenêtres", or "The Windows". The poem is built like one of Delaunay's paintings, with bright pieces of the world placed next to one another. On 24 December 1913, at the Sorbonne, the language scholar Ferdinand Brunot recorded Apollinaire's voice on a phonograph. The recordings were made for Brunot's new "archives of speech". They still exist. People today can hear Apollinaire reading "Le Pont Mirabeau", "Marie", and "Le Voyageur". In March 1913, Apollinaire published Les Peintres cubistes. Méditations esthétiques, or "The Cubist Painters: Aesthetic Meditations". It was not a cold or difficult book of theory. It was a poet's book about painting. Apollinaire wrote about Picasso, Braque, Jean Metzinger, Albert Gleizes, Marie Laurencin, Juan Gris, Fernand Léger, Picabia, and Duchamp. He explained the main idea of modern art in a clear and bold way. A modern painting did not have to copy nature like a photograph. Music could be true without copying an object, and painting could do the same. The book made Apollinaire, in the eyes of the public, the official voice of Cubism. He followed every new art movement in Europe. In the summer of 1913, he published a manifesto for the Italian Futurists called L'Antitradition futuriste. A manifesto is a public statement of ideas. This wild printed sheet offered roses to the people who invented new things. It also shouted the half-printed insult "MER…DE" at professors, museums, and critics. Some of Apollinaire's friends were shocked. In fact, he was partly joking. He shared the Futurists' love of machines, cities, and games with printed words. However, he did not share their hatred of the past. His own work showed the opposite idea: the newest poetry could carry all the old stories and legends inside it. In April 1913, the publisher Mercure de France published Apollinaire's first major collection of poems, Alcools, or "Alcohols" and "Spirits". He was thirty-two years old. The book contained about fifty poems written during fifteen years. The oldest came from his year in the Rhineland in 1901 and 1902. The newest was "Zone", which he had finished only a few months before the book was printed. The title means strong drink, but it also suggests fire and life. For Apollinaire, the modern world itself was like alcohol. It burned people and made them drunk. Near the end of "Zone", the first poem in the book, the poet drinks his own life like burning brandy. In "Vendémiaire", the final poem, he describes himself as drunk because he has drunk the whole universe. At the front of the book was something very unusual for a poetry collection: a Cubist portrait of Apollinaire drawn by Picasso. The face was made of broken lines and flat shapes. Many readers thought the portrait was a joke. For Apollinaire, it was the perfect image of the collection. It joined order with adventure and tradition with invention. When Apollinaire read the first proofs of Alcools at the end of 1912, he made a bold choice. He removed every comma, every full stop, and every other punctuation mark from the whole book. A few poets, including Stéphane Mallarmé, had already tried this in single poems. The Futurists had also asked poets to do it in their manifestos. However, removing punctuation from a complete poetry collection was still very unusual. It attracted much attention. A critic asked Apollinaire why he had done this. In a letter written in July 1913, he answered that punctuation was useless. He wrote: "le rythme même et la coupe des vers voilà la véritable ponctuation", meaning that the rhythm and the division of the lines were the real punctuation. He also removed other parts of the poems. More than fifty lines disappeared from the manuscript of "Zone" before the book was printed. He also removed names of places and dates that made the poems seem too private. Without punctuation, each line can stand by itself. Words may connect with the line before or with the line after it. One sentence can therefore have two meanings at the same time. The famous beginning of "Le Pont Mirabeau" shows this: (Under the Mirabeau Bridge flows the Seine / And our loves) Do "our loves" flow away with the river, or do the words begin the next sentence? Both readings can be true at the same time. After Alcools, poetry without punctuation became common in many languages. It remains common today. Alcools contains many different voices. It begins with "Zone", the newest poem, and ends with "Vendémiaire", a great song of praise to Paris. The poems between them are not placed in the order in which they were written. The order of the poems is itself part of the art. The scholar Marie-Jeanne Durry noticed that "L'Émigrant de Landor Road", the poem about Annie's departure, is placed at the exact centre of the book. The same number of poems comes before it and after it. For Durry, this quiet arrangement shows that Apollinaire's lost English love remained at the centre of his inner life. "Zone" is a long walk through Paris and through the poet's whole life. It begins in the morning and ends the next morning. Its first line is one of the best-known lines in modern French poetry: À la fin tu es las de ce monde ancien, or "In the end, you are tired of this ancient world". The poem praises aeroplanes, posters, typists, and advertising papers as the true poetry of modern life. It then moves through Apollinaire's memories: his religious childhood, Prague, London, his lost loves, and the poor people leaving their countries at the Saint-Lazare station. It ends at sunrise with two strange short lines: Adieu Adieu / Soleil cou coupé, or "Farewell Farewell / Sun cut throat". The red rising sun is seen as a cut neck. Readers have connected this image with the cut heads and burning suns in his poems of 1908. "Le Pont Mirabeau" is a slow and sad song about the end of his love for Marie Laurencin. Time and love pass like the river. Only the poet remains. "La Chanson du mal-aimé" is his long London poem for Annie Playden. It mixes his own story with Ulysses, the Cossacks of Zaporozhia, and the queens of legend. "Marie" is a song about two women at the same time. The Marie who dances the maclotte, a folk dance from the Ardennes, is Mareye of Stavelot. The Marie whom the poet asks to return is Marie Laurencin. The "Rhénanes" are the German poems. They are filled with night, wine, travelling people, and drowned voices. "Les Colchiques", or "The Autumn Crocuses", compares the eyes of the loved woman to a beautiful but poisonous flower. "Cortège", "Le Brasier", and "Les Fiançailles" are difficult and powerful poems. In them, the poet burns his old self and is born again. Apollinaire believed that "Les Fiançailles", which he dedicated to Picasso, was one of his best works. The shortest poem in the book, "Chantre", or "Singer", has only one line. Old and new appear side by side throughout the collection. Strict classical verse stands next to free verse. Church bells stand next to aeroplanes. Merlin stands next to the Eiffel Tower. This mixture was exactly what Apollinaire wanted. The reviews were divided. Some critics praised the music and beauty of the book. Others mocked it or became angry. The strongest attack came from the poet Georges Duhamel in the Mercure de France in June 1913. He wrote that the collection looked like a second-hand shop. It was, he said, a pile of used objects, some valuable, but none made by the shopkeeper himself. Duhamel also attacked Apollinaire's mixed foreign origins with words that today clearly show hatred of foreigners. Apollinaire was deeply hurt. For a short time, he even thought about challenging Duhamel to a duel. Many years later, Duhamel said that he regretted the review. Younger readers reacted very differently. For many poets born around 1895, Alcools soon became a model and a place to begin. Today, it is one of the most studied works of French poetry. Marie-Jeanne Durry wrote several volumes of university lectures about it, and many books explain the poems one by one. In 1914, Apollinaire began to draw pictures with words. On 15 June 1914, Les Soirées de Paris published "Lettre-Océan", or "Ocean-Letter". It was the first of his visual poems. At first, he called such poems "idéogrammes lyriques", or "lyric ideograms". An ocean-letter was a real form of message at that time. It was sent between ships at sea by the new wireless telegraph. "Lettre-Océan" covers two full pages. Its words form two large wheels with lines like spokes. They look like radio waves spreading from the Eiffel Tower. The reader's eyes can follow the words in several directions. Inside the two wheels are parts of a letter to Apollinaire's brother Albert in Mexico. There are also street cries from Paris, ship sirens, and the calls of a bus driver. All these sounds happen at the same time. The scholar Willard Bohn describes it as a poem that must be seen all at once, like a picture, rather than read only one line after another. The Italian Futurists had experimented with the printed shape of words a few months earlier, and Apollinaire learned from them. However, one month later he published four more picture-poems that were completely his own: "Voyage", "Paysage animé", "La Cravate et la montre", and "Cœur couronne et miroir". These were real drawings made from words. They showed a heart, a crown, a mirror, a necktie, a watch, and a smoking cigar. Apollinaire planned to collect them in a book called Et moi aussi je suis peintre, or "I Too Am a Painter". The war stopped the project. The book was finally published only in 2006. In 1917, Apollinaire invented a new and beautiful name for these poems: calligrammes. The word comes from Greek words meaning "beautiful" and "writing". Many critics complained. They asked whether this was still poetry or only a childish game. Apollinaire answered that he was bringing back a very old tradition, which went back to ancient Greece. He also believed that he was pointing toward a future in which poetry, drawing, and cinema would come together. At the end of July 1914, Apollinaire was in Deauville, on the coast of Normandy. He was writing a light newspaper report with his friend, the artist André Rouveyre. On 31 July, as war came very close, the two men drove through the night back to Paris. France ordered a general mobilization the next day. Within a few days, the First World War had begun. Apollinaire did not have to fight. He was not a French citizen. He was officially a Russian subject who had been born in Rome, so France could not force him to join its army. He chose to fight. On 5 August 1914, he asked to join the army. In September, he also asked to become a French citizen. The army was slow to deal with foreign volunteers. While he waited, Apollinaire went to Nice. On 4 December 1914, he finally signed an agreement to serve "for the duration of the war". On 6 December, he entered the 38th field artillery regiment at Nîmes as an ordinary gunner. The historian Annette Becker notes that his military papers use the word "engagement" three times on two pages. In French, this word means a soldier's free decision to serve. Apollinaire was thirty-four years old. He was older and heavier than most new soldiers, but he trained seriously. He rode horses for six hours a day and learned to use the French 75-mm gun. Half as a joke, he told his friends that being a soldier seemed to be his true profession. In Nice, at the end of September 1914, Apollinaire met Louise de Coligny-Châtillon.

Guillermo Díaz Rodriguez (born January 27, 1971), widely known as Guillermo, is a talk show personality who rose to fame while working as a parking lot security guard at the Hollywood Blvd studios for Jimmy Kimmel Live!, with Jimmy Kimmel.

Guillermo Mordillo (4 August 1932 – 29 June 2019), known simply as Mordillo, was an Argentine cartoonist and animator. He was born in Buenos Aires. Mordillo was one of the most widely published cartoonists of the 1970s. He was known for creating greeting cards for Hallmark Cards. From 1976 to 1981, Mordillo's cartoons were used by Slovenian artist Miki Muster to create Mordillo, a series of 400 short animations that were later presented at Cannes and bought by television studios from 30 countries. Mordillo died on 30 June 2019 in Palma de Mallorca, Spain at the age of 86.

Guillermo Kahlo (born Carl Wilhelm Kahlo; 26 October 1871 – 14 April 1941) was a German-Mexican photographer. He was known for photographic architectural works, churches, streets, landmarks, as well as industries and companies in Mexico at the beginning of the 20th century in Mexico. He was the father of painter Frida Kahlo.

Guillermo Rodríguez Melgarejo (20 May 1943 – 4 January 2021) was an Argentine Roman Catholic bishop. Melgarejo was born in Buenos Aires, Argentina. He became a priest in 1970. Melgarejo was titular bishop of Ucres and as auxiliary bishop of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Buenos Aires from 1994 to 2003 and as bishop of the Roman Catholic Diocese of San Martín in Argentina from 2003 to 2018. Melgarejo died on 4 January 2021, aged 77.

Guillermo Sepúlveda Rodríguez (29 November 1934 – 19 May 2021) was a Mexican football defender. He played for Mexico in the 1958 and 1962 FIFA World Cups. He also played for C.D. Guadalajara. Sepúlveda died on 19 May 2021 in Mexico City, aged 86.

Guillermo Eduardo Díaz Zambrano (29 December 1930 – 25 September 1997) was a Chilean football midfielder. He played for Chile in the 1950 FIFA World Cup. He made nineteen appearances from 1950 until 1957.

Guity Novin (born Guity Navran on April 21, 1944) is a Persian-Canadian painter and sculptor. She has started a movement in painting that she has named Transpressionism. She was born in Kermanshah, Iran in 1944. She now lives and works in Vancouver and Toronto. Guity Novin was graduated from the Faculty of Fine Arts in Tehran in 1970. After leaving Iran, she moved to The Hague, Netherlands in 1975 and then to Manchester, UK where she completed her studies. She moved to Canada in 1980 and lived and exhibited in Kingston (Ontario), Montreal, and Ottawa and finally settled in Vancouver, British Columbia. She has introduced the Transpressionism style in 1994. By using this style, she tries to convey her passionate philosophical ideas. She has served on a UNESCO national committee of artists.

Gul Mohamad Zhowandai (1905-1988) was born in Kabul, Afghanistan. He was a poet and writer. He wrote novels in Persian. His published works include: Ferroz — short stories (Kabul, Afghanistan) Ahrezo ah ye per ahshoob — short stories (Kabul, Afghanistan: Islla Publications) Collection of Poems (Kabul, Afghanistan: Islla, Anis)
Sardar Gujjar Singh Bhangi (died early 1790) was a Sikh warrior and one of the triumvirates who ruled over Lahore prior to the leadership of Maharaja Ranjit Singh.

Gukesh Dommaraju (born 29 May 2006), also known as Gukesh D, is an Indian chess grandmaster who is the current World Chess Champion. He is the youngest World Chess Champion and the youngest Candidates Tournament winner. He was also the third-youngest grandmaster and the youngest to reach a rating of 2750. He has won one team and two individual gold medals at the 2024 45th Chess Olympiad. Gukesh is also a silver medalist at the Asian Games. On December 12, 2024, he won against Chinese grandmaster Ding Liren in the World Chess Championship, officially becoming the youngest FIDE World Champion ever.

Ismail Gulgee (commonly known as just Gulgee) (October 25, 1926 – December 16, 2007) was a Pakistani artist born in Peshawar. He was a qualified engineer and a self-taught abstract artist and portrait painter. Exhibitions of his work were held in many countries around the world, including the United Kingdom, United States, Iran, United Arab Emirates, France and other countries.

Gulnazar Keldi (; 20 September 1945 – 13 August 2020) was a Tajikistani poet. He was born in Dardar He was an editor of the publication Adabiyet va sanat (Literature and Art). Keldi wrote the lyrics of Surudi Milli, the national anthem of Tajikistan. Keldi died on 13 August 2020 in Dushanbe from COVID-19, aged 74.

Gunnar Hultgren (19 February 1902, Eskilstuna, Sweden – 13 February 1991, Uppsala, Sweden) was a Swedish bishop. He was active within the Church of Sweden. He was the Archbishop of Uppsala between 1958 and 1967.

Gunnar Birkerts (, January 17, 1925 – August 15, 2017) was a Latvian-American architect. He was born in Riga, Latvia. For most of his career, Birkerts was based in the metropolitan area of Detroit, Michigan. Some of his designs include the Corning Museum of Glass and the Corning Fire Station in Corning, New York, Marquette Plaza in Minneapolis, Minnesota, the Kemper Museum of Contemporary Art in Kansas City, Missouri, and the U.S. Embassy in Caracas, Venezuela. In 2014, he designed the National Library of Latvia in Riga, Latvia, aka the Castle of Light, whose architectural form references and draws inspiration from Latvian folklore. Birkerts died at the age of 92 on August 15, 2017 at his home in Needham, Massachusetts of congestive heart failure.

Gunnar Ernst Algot Sandgren (27 June 1929 – 4 November 2016) was a Swedish novelist and playwright. He made his literary debut in 1960, with the novel Förklaringsberget. He later wrote a series of historical novels. He was awarded the Dobloug Prize in 1981. Sandgren died on 4 November 2016 at the age of 87.

Karl Gunnar Myrdal (; 6 December 1898 – 17 May 1987) was a Swedish economist and sociologist. In 1974, he received the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences with Friedrich Hayek for their work in the theory of money and economic fluctuations. He was best known in the United States for his study of race relations, which is seen in his book An American Dilemma: The Negro Problem and Modern Democracy.

Ellen Gunilla Margareta Pontén (14 June 1929 – 29 June 2019) was a Swedish fashion designer. She was born in Stockholm. Pontén designed clothes with the base colours of grey, white or black. In 1983, she was awarded the Damernas Värld design award Guldknappen, in 2003 she was awarded a Litteris et Artibus In 2008, she was awarded the KTH Great Prize. Pontén died on 29 June 2019, in Stockholm at the age of 90.

Gunnar Fischer (November 18, 1910 – June 11, 2011) was a Swedish cinematographer and writer. He is known for having filmed several movies directed by Ingmar Bergman. He was married to the sister of Åke Söderblom.

Gunilla Elisabet Dukure Bergström (3 July 1942 – 25 August 2021) was a Swedish author, journalist, and illustrator. She was best known for her series of children's books about the character Alfie Atkins. She was born in Gothenburg, Sweden. Bergström died on 25 August 2021 in Stockholm, Sweden at the age of 79.

Gunnar Utterberg (28 November 1942 – 12 September 2021) was a Swedish sprint canoer. He was born in Jönköping, Sweden. He competed in 1000 m doubles and fours at the 1964, 1968 and 1972 Olympics. He won a gold medal in the doubles event in 1964. Utterbeg died on 12 September 2021, at the age of 78.
Gunnar Jervill (born 23 November 1945 in Gothenburg) is a Swedish archer. Gunnar competed at the 1972 Summer Olympics and at the 1976 Summer Olympics.

Gunnar Weman (25 February 1932 – 24 February 2024) was a Swedish priest who was the Archbishop of Uppsala from 1993 to 1997. Weman died on 24 February 2024 in Sigtuna, Sweden, the day before his 92nd birthday.

Gunnel Vallquist (19 June 1918 – 11 January 2016) was a Swedish writer and translator. She became a member of the Swedish Academy in 1982. She wrote over twenty books. She also translated In Search of Lost Time by Marcel Proust from French into Swedish. She was born in Stockholm. Vallquist died on 11 January 2016, aged 97.

Guo Jianmei (Simplified Chinese: 郭建梅; Hanyu pinyin Guō Jiànméi; born October 1961) is a Chinese lawyer and human rights activist. She is the head of an organization to help women with legal problems. In 2011, she received the International Women of Courage Award from the United States Department of State. Guo Jianmei was born in a poor area of Hua County, Henan Province, in China. Both her parents were teachers. Guo saw poverty and problems with women's rights in her village. This gave her the idea to work for women's rights in China. She is married to writer Liu Zhenyun. When she was 18, Guo went to law school at Beijing University. She graduated in 1983. After she graduated, she worked at the Ministry of Justice, The All China Federation of Women, and The All China Association of Lawyers. In 1989, Guo helped to write the law on the Protection of Women's Rights and Interests. Guo traveled to more than 20 areas of China to learn about the lives of Chinese women. In 1995, Guo went to the Fourth World Conference on Women in Beijing. When a foreign lawyer asked about non-governmental organizations to help women with legal problems, everyone was silent. They understood that women had very little help in China. Later that year, Guo and her friends started the Beijing University Law School Women's Legal Research and Services Centre, China's first NGO non-governmental organization for legal help for women. Guo helped write China's new marriage law in 2001. In 2003, she helped write the law for Regulations for Legal Aid. Guo wrote 8 books. She is also editor of three volumes of "Everyday Life Law", and "A Guide to Women's Legal Aid Cases". In 2010 Guo Jianmei received the Simone De Beauvoir Prize. Also in 2010, the International Labor Organisation (ILO) named her China’s first anti-AIDS discrimination ambassador. In 2011 she received the International Women of Courage Award from the United States Department of State.

Gunther Rolf Kress MBE (03 March 1940 – 20 June 2019) was an Australian semiotician working at a British University. Kress was born in Germany and trained as a linguist in Australia. He was Professor of Semiotics and Education at the Institute of Education, University of London. Kress named a Member of the Order of the British Empire (MBE) in 2012. Kress died in Rome on 20 June 2019 of heart failure. He was 79.

Guo Shoujing (, 1231–1316), or Ruosi (若思), was a Chinese astronomer, engineer, and mathematician. He lived during the Yuan Dynasty (1271–1368). He is considered one of the greatest scientists in Chinese history. Guo was a major influence in the development of science. He improved the Grand Canal, built a human-made lake (Kunming lake), created one of the most accurate calendars in history, invented some of the most accurate clocks during his time, and made many other contributions to math, astronomy, and hydraulics (water engineering). He was born in 1231 in Xingtai, Hebei province. His family was poor. His grandfather, Guo Yong, was famous for his study of the Five Classics to astronomy, mathematics, and hydraulics. Guo Shoujing was a child prodigy. As a teenager, he learned how to build a water clock. He then improved it. His new invention was called the lotus clepsydra (a bowl shaped like a lotus flower that water dripped into). At 16 he began to study math and from there hydraulics and astronomy. At 20, Guo became a hydraulic engineer and government official. He helped fix a bridge over the Dahuoquan River. In the late 1250s, Kublai Khan (of the Mongol Empire, Yuan dynasty) thought hydraulic engineering, irrigation, and water transport would help the country and people. He sent Liu Bingzhong and his student Guo to improve irrigation systems between Dadu (now Beijing) and the Yellow River. Guo helped build a 30 km canal from Baifu spring in the Shenshan Mountain to Dadu, The Grand Canal linked the Yangzi river, the Huai, and Yellow river since the early 7th century. Guo helped extend it to Dadu 1292–93. It worked. Kublai Khan was happy, and Guo did similar things for the rest of the empire. He was promoted to chief advisor of hydraulics, mathematics, and astronomy. He created a human-made Kunming Lake in Beijing. This was one of his most memorable engineering feats. The lake provided water for all areas surrounding Beijing and led to the best grain transport system in the world. He built other reservoirs, thereby allowing people in inner China to access to fresh water for planting, drinking, and trading. For irrigation, he provided hydraulics systems which distributed water equally and quickly, which allowed communities to trade more effectively, and therefore prosper. In 1292, he became the head of the Water Works Bureau. Guo invented many astronomy devices: the gnomon, the square table, the armilla, and a water powered armillary sphere called the Ling Long Yi. The gnomon is a clock; it tells the time by measuring the position sun (like a sundial). It can also determine the seasons. Guo made this device much more accurate. The square table measures the angle and position of stars in the side. It is also a protractor. The armilla measures the angle of the sun, as well as the position of any celestial body. The Ling Long Yi is a fancier and more accurate version of the armilla. Even when young Guo was revolutionizing old inventions. His clocks, watches, irrigation, reservoirs, and equilibrium stations were the most accurate of his time, allowing for an extremely accurate recording of time. Kublai Khan noticed Guo was a genius in astronomy. So he asked Guo, Zhang, and Wang Xun to build a very accurate calendar. It would be the most accurate of its time. They built 27 observatories in the empire to collect data for calculations. In 1280, Guo finished the calendar, calculating a year to be 365.2425 days, just 26 seconds off modern measurements. He invented many tools in the process. The calendar revolutionized China and the world. It allowed more accurate recording of history, gave a sense of unification, and helped later emperors rule over China. His calendar would be used for the next 363 years, the longest a Chinese calendar has been used in history. Guo was also able to more accurately establish the location of celestial bodies and the angles of the Sun relative to Earth. He invented a new type of compass, helping people find north using the stars instead of magnets. In 1283, Guo was promoted to director of the Observatory in Beijing. Guo’s work in mathematics was regarded as the most knowledgeable for 400 years. Throughout his life he worked a lot on spherical trigonometry, using a system of approximation to find arc lengths and angles. He approximated pi was equal to 3. But this allowed him to solve some equations much faster and more accurately than if he said pi was 3.14.... He also used mathematical functions for spherical trigonometry, building upon the knowledge of Shen Kuo's (1031–1095). The next important work in trigonometry would only be printed 300 years later by Xu Guangqi in 1607, during the Ming Dynasty. Tang Shunzhi 唐順之 (1507-1560) said Guo's work was an example of "practical scholarship" (applying advanced knowledge to solve practical problems). Guo influenced the Changzhou School of Thought and spread of "evidential learning" (learning through experience). A number of things are named after Guo, including the Asteroid 2012 Guo Shou-Jing and the Large Sky Area Multi-Object Fibre Spectroscopic Telescope near Beijing.

Gunther Kaschlun (9 February 1935 – 7 August 2020) was a West German rower. He represented the United Team of Germany. He competed at the 1956 Summer Olympics in Melbourne with the men's coxless four where they were eliminated in the semi-final. He died in August 2020 at the age of 85.

Guo Xiliang (22 September 1930 – 30 December 2022) was a Chinese linguist and professor. Guo educated at the Hunan University, Wuhan University and Peking University. He was professor and doctoral supervisor of the at the Peking University. Guo Xiliang died in Beijing on 30 December 2022, at the age of 92.

George Ivanovich Gurdjieff (13 January 1866 – 29 October 1949), usually called Gurdjieff, was a Greek- Armenian guru and writer. He was an influential spiritual teacher of the first half of the 20th century. He was influenced by Sufi, Zen and Yoga mystics he met on his early travels. Gurdjieff taught that most people live their entire lives in a state of hypnotic "waking sleep": "Speaking frankly... contemporary man as we know him is nothing more than merely a clockwork mechanism, though of a very complex construction". "A modern man lives in sleep, in sleep he is born and in sleep he dies".p66 Gurdjieff developed a method for working towards a higher state of consciousness and achieving full human potential. He called this "The Work" or "The Method". Gurdjieff's method for awakening one's consciousness is different from that of the fakir, monk or yogi, so his discipline was called originally the "Fourth Way". At different times in his life, Gurdjieff started and closed various schools around the world to teach the work. He said that the teachings he brought to the West came from his own experiences and early travels. The teachings expressed the truth found in ancient religions. They were wisdom teachings relating to self-awareness in people's daily lives, and humanity's place in the universe. Gurdjieff G.I. 1950. Beelzebub's tales to his grandson: an objectively impartial criticism of the life of man. 3 vols, Routledge & Kegan Paul, London. 1973 reprint, E.P. Dutton, N.Y. Gurdjieff G.I. 1957. The struggle of the magicians: scenario of the ballet. Stourton, Capetown. Very limited printing of ten copies. Gurdjieff G.I. 1963. Meetings with remarkable men. Routledge & Kegan Paul, London.. Gurdjieff's own autobiography Gurjieff G.I. 1975. Life is only real then, when "I am". Routledge & Kegan Paul, London. Ouspensky P.D. 1950. In search of the miraculous: fragments of an unknown teaching. Routledge & Kegan Paul, London. "Substantially, this comprises Gurdjieff's direct speech, which Gurdjieff gratefully acknowledged". Moore's biography p403. Ouspensky P.D. 1957. The fourth way: a record of talks and answers to questions based on the teaching of G.I. Gurdjieff. Routledge & Kegan Paul, London. Routledge & Kegan Paul, London. Bennett J.G. 1973. Gurdjieff: making a new world. Routledge & Kegan Paul, London. Bennett J.G. 1975. Witness: the autobiography of John Bennett. Turnstone, London.. Moore, James 1991. Gurdjieff: a biography. Element, Shaftesbury, Dorset. Smoley R. & Kinney J. 2006. Hidden wisdom: a guide to the western inner traditions. Wheaton, Illinois: Quest Books.. Chapter 9 (The way of the sly man: the teachings of G.I. Gurdjieff) is an excellent introduction to Gurdjieff. There is a 1979 British film, Meetings with Remarkable Men, directed by Peter Brook. It is based on the book of the same name by Gurdjieff. It was shot on location in Afghanistan (except for dance sequences, which were filmed in England). It starred Terence Stamp as Prince Lubovedsky, and Dragan Maksimovic as the adult Gurdjieff. The film was entered into the 29th Berlin International Film Festival and nominated for the Golden Bear prize.

Gurdon Saltonstall Hubbard (August 22, 1802 in Windsor, Vermont – September 14, 1886 in Chicago, Illinois) was an American fur trader, insurance underwriter and land speculator. Hubbard first arrived in Chicago on October 1, 1818 as a voyageur. He went on to build Chicago's first stockyard and help form a land boom for Chicago in the East.

Guram Dochanashvili (; 26 March 1939 – 3 April 2021) was a Georgian writer and historian. He was popular for his short stories, beginning in the 1960s. He was known for his The First Garment book series. Dochanashvili was hospitalized on 1 April 2021 in Tbilisi. His condition was critical and he died two days later, aged 82.

The Gurevich brothers were Russian-born Jewish partisans. Their names were Khaim Gurevich (born in or in ) and Lev Gurevich (born on 20 September 1926). In Nazi Germany, they led the Gurevich partisan unit, which smuggled Jewish teenage boys from the Petrovichi Ghetto in Smolensk Oblast and trained them to fight. Beginning on 21 July 1942, the Gurevich partisans began smuggling Jewish young men from the Petrovichi Ghetto into a refugee camp they established in the nearby forest. There, the partisans trained the young men to use weapons, grenades, and explosives. They also taught them how to sabotage the Nazis by removing pieces from train tracks to derail Nazi trains. The partisans used these techniques whenever Nazi German soldiers approached the camp planning to kill the people there. Along with fighting techniques, the young men learned how to survive in the forest and how to steal supplies (like food, water, ammunition, weaponry, first aid supplies, and medicine). The partisans were sometimes given food, water, and medicine by Russian partisans, soldiers, and other people who passed by their camp in the forest. These people never betrayed the partisans of the Nazis. Ultimately, Khaim and Lev Gurevich saved about 30 Jewish teenage boys from the Petrovichi Ghetto. During a fight with Nazi soldiers, Lev was seriously wounded in the leg. People in the refugee camp nursed Lev until, sometime between 22 December 1942 and 21 January 1943, a Russian married couple discovered the camp. After speaking with Khaim, the couple took Lev into their home, hiding him in a hole inside their cellar. They cared for Lev and brought him food and water while he hid. Lev received excellent care for eight months, until the Soviet Bolshevik Red Army liberated Smolensk Oblast and drove the Nazis away in late September 1943. At some point, the Russian wife was executed by hanging. Historians are unsure exactly when she was hanged or why. Soviet soldiers may have murdered her during or after the war. Alternatively, she might have been killed by Nazi officers, perhaps because they found out Lev was hiding in their house but could not find him. It is unclear why her husband was not executed as well. (Small note: Lev Gurevich is not to be mistaken for Dr. Lev Gurevich, doctor and violinist from Moscow.).

Guru Nanak Dev (15 April 1469 – 22 September 1539) was the founder of Sikhism and is regarded as its first Guru. Guru Nanak was born in Rāi Bhoi Dī Talvaṇḍī, in Punjab. This is now part of Pakistan. Guru Nanak came from a Hindu landowning family, with his father known as Mehta Kalu and his mother as Mata Tripta. When Guru Nanak was a child he refused the upanayana (holy thread) to initiate him into the Hindu religion. Later in his life he married Mata Sulakhani with whom he had two sons. They were called Sri Chand and Lakshmi Das. According to the Sikh religion, one day he was bathing in the river and god took him up to heaven. His family members were very worried as they had thought he died. After three days, he returned with the message of god. He gave up his job to spread the message on how to be a good person. Guru Nanak died in Kartarpur.

Shri Guru Angad Dev Ji (, 1504 - Sept 7, 1539) was one of the ten gurus who founded Sikhism. He became a Guru because of the obedience he showed to his Guru (Guru Nanak,the first guru in Sikh religion). Guru Angad Dev invented the present form of the Gurmukhi script.

Guru Ram Das (24 September 1534 in Lahore, Punjab, Pakistan – 1 September 1581, in Amritsar, Punjab, India) was the fourth of the ten Sikh Gurus on 26 March 1552.
