He urged Sikhs to not just sit in peace while meditating. He urged them to actively join in with other peoples fun while meditating. Guru Ram Das nominated Guru Arjun Dev, his youngest son, as the next Guru of the Sikhs. Guru Ram helped build Ramdaspur by digging a second sacred pool after being instructed to do so by Guru Amar Das. Pilgrims came from miles to hear Guru Ram preach or to help him dig the sacred pool. The sacred pool (Holy tank) was named Amristar - which means great pool of nectar.

Guru Arjan Dev (15 April 1563 – 30 May 1606) was the fifth of the ten human Sikh gurus. He became a Guru on September 1st 1556. He laid down the foundations for the Harmandir sahib, which is popularly known as “The Golden Temple”. It was built in the middle of the second sacred [pool] in Ramdaspur that was the tallest building in the town. He thought that it should not be the tallest building in town so he ordered it to be built on the lowest point in the pool. He helped build a lot of buildings around and dug wells and laid more foundations for other buildings around the Golden temple. Guru Arjan was arrested under the orders of the Mughal Emperor Jahangir, who accused him of supporting a rebellion under Khusrau Mirza. The emperor demanded that he convert to Islam, but he refused, so he was tortured and executed in 1606. Historical records and the Sikh tradition are unclear as to whether Arjan was executed by drowning or died during torture. The Sikh tradition states the Guru's execution was a part of the ongoing persecution of the Sikhs under the Mughal Empire. His martyrdom is considered a watershed event in the history of Sikhism. It is remembered as Shaheedi Divas of Guru Arjan in May or June according to the Nanakshahi calendar released by the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee in 2003.

Guru Har Krishan (; 23 July 1656 – 30 March 1664) was the eighth of the ten gurus of Sikhism. He became Guru on 7 October 1661, on the death of his father, Guru Har Rai. Due to the smallpox epidemic that was happening at that time, Guru Har Krishan died at the young age of 7. His grand-uncle, Guru Tegh Bahadur, became the next Guru of the Sikhs.

Augustus Cornelius "Gus" Johnson, Jr. (born August 10, 1967) is an American television sportscaster. He works for Fox College Football as the lead play by play announcer. He is well known for his yelling and screaming emotions on exciting plays. He was also employed by Showtime, and the Big Ten Network. He was employed by CBS Sports. He was also a play-by-play announcer for the Minnesota Timberwolves. He called Big East basketball for ESPN Plus, college basketball and college hockey for ESPN. He hosted Black College Sports Today in 1991. Johnson called Canadian Football League games for ESPN. He also called NFL games for CBS until 2011. Johnson was first paired up with Steve Tasker, then Brent Jones. He got back together with Steve Tasker in 2005 until his departure for Fox Sports in 2011. He had sports anchor stints on KXXV-TV, WAAY-TV, WXII-TV, and WTTG-TV. He called college basketball tournaments for CBS for many years. He had many partners including Dan Bonner, Len Elmore, and Bill Raftery. He was also the radio voice and back-up television play-by-play announcer for the New York Knicks. He was well known for calling Allan Houston's game winning buzzer beater to knock off the top seeded Miami Heat. He called boxing for MSG as well as hosting Knicks GameNight and Yankees Scorecard. He was the studio host for New York Rangers telecasts. Johnson was a preseason voice in 2006 for the Buffalo Bills and the Philadelphia Eagles. He was the preseason voice of the Detroit Lions for the Detroit Lions Television Network in 2008. Johnson replaced Steve Albert as lead play-by-play announcer for Showtime Championship Boxing and called Strikeforce for CBS Sports Spectacular. He also called games for the defunct arena football New York Dragons. He calls NFL and college football games on Fox with Charles Davis. Johnson also calls college basketball games for the Big Ten Network and worked a few road games for the San Jose Earthquakes of Major League Soccer.

Virgil Ivan "Gus" Grissom (April 3, 1926 – January 27, 1967) was an American test pilot and astronaut. He was one of the original seven astronauts selected for NASA's Project Mercury in April 1959. On July 21, 1961, Grissom flew into space in the Liberty Bell 7 spacecraft. This was powered by a Redstone rocket. Grissom was the second American in space, following Alan Shepard. He made another space flight as command pilot (pilot in charge) of Gemini 3. This was the first trip by astronauts in NASA's Project Gemini. The trip took place on March 23, 1965. Grissom died along with fellow astronauts Ed White and Roger Chaffee during a test for the Apollo 1 mission at Cape Canaveral Air Force Station (then known as Cape Kennedy), Florida. He was the first of the Mercury Seven to die.

Augustus Edwards (born 13 April 1995) is a Liberian American football running back. He plays for the Baltimore Ravens of the National Football League (NFL). He was recruited out of Tottenville High School as a three-star recruit by both ESPN and Rivals.com. Edwards started his career by playing college football at Miami. He would play with the Hurricanes from 2013 until 2016. In 2017, he transferred to Rutgers to play his final year in college. Edwards would go undrafted. On 4 May 2018, the Baltimore Ravens would sign Edwards along with 14 other undrafted rookies. On 15 October, Edwards would make his NFL debut with the Ravens in a 21–0 win against the Tennessee Titans. In the game, he was able to record his 42 yards on 10 carries. In his debut year, Edwards would finish the 2018 season with 718 rushing yards and 2 touchdowns. He was fifth in rookie running backs in the league. On 25 November 2018, Edwards would become the first Ravens rookie since Jamal Lewis in 2000 to have back-to-back 100+ yard rushing games. On 7 June 2021, Edwards would sign a two-year; $10 million contract extension with the Ravens. Edwards was born on 13 April 1995 in Monrovia, Liberia. He was born during the First Liberian Civil War. His family would move to New York when Edwards was five years old.

Guru Brahmanand (24 December 1908 - 16 May 1973), also known as Jagatguru Swami Brahmanand Saraswati Ji, was an Indian guru, social reformer and philosopher. He is widely known in state of Haryana for his efforts in promoting education, social equality, and spiritual awareness. Brahmanand's birthday, 24 December, is commemorated in Haryana as Guru Brahmanand Jayanti or Brahmanand Jayanti, a restricted holiday in Haryana. He was born as Chhotaram on 24 December 1908 in Chuhar Majra, Kaithal district, Haryana. He was born to Badama Ram and Rami Devi, and brought up in a Haryanvi Samdhyan clan of Ror caste. His father, Badama Ram, was a farmer. His mother Rami Devi died when he was 9 years old and when he was 11 years old, his father Badama Ram passed away. He departed his village and embarked on a pilgrimage across the Northern India. He travelled for some years and made observations on contemporary social life. In his quest for true knowledge, he went to the forests of Sapta Sarovar, beyond Haridwar, for penance. There, he decided to leave his mortal body, and as he did so, three goddesses appeared and presented him with a five-colored Panchranga flag. The three goddesses named him Brahmanand because he remained absorbed in Brahma Anand (divine bliss). He established five principles for the five-colored Panchranga flag, and upon returning, he founded a gurukul called Ompura. After a few years, he set out to propagate the Vedic religion and organized more than 200 Havan Yagnas and Bhandaras (community feasts) across the region. He established many ashrams in various villages of Haryana. Brahmanand moved all across the Northern India and usually resided in villages. Some of these are listed below. On 16 May 1973, he left his mortal body at his Fatehpur Ashram, after chanting Om three times, and attained liberation. Brahmamand served as an inspiration for several Indian thinkers and social reformers. Brahmanand is a revered religious and spiritual figure in the Indian state of Haryana and remains relevant to present-day society due to his enduring spiritual contributions. His teachings and philosophy have been promoted and endorsed by various political and social organizations in Haryana. Many public institutions and places are named in his honour, and the Guru Brahmanand Ji Government Polytechnic, Nilokheri. Guru Brahmanand Kanya Mahavidyalaya, Anjanthali, Karnal, Guru Brahmanand Chowk, Karnal is also named in his honour.

Gustav Robert Kirchhoff (12 March 1824 – 17 October 1887) was a German physicist who contributed to the fundamental understanding of electrical circuits, spectroscopy, and radiation by heated objects. He coined the term black body radiation in 1862. He proposed two sets of independent concepts in both circuit theory and thermal emission. They are all called 'Kirchhoff's laws' after him, as well as a law of thermochemistry. The Bunsen–Kirchhoff Award for spectroscopy is named after him and his colleague, Robert Bunsen. He also discovered rubidium with Bunsen in 1861.

Gustav Gerneth (15 October 1905 – 21 October 2019) was a German World War II-veteran and possibly the oldest man ever in Germany, as well as the world's oldest man at the time of his death. However, his age is not validated by Guinness World Records and the Gerontology Research Group. Gerneth worked in a shipping company and at a gas plant during World War II. He was a Soviet prisoner-of-war until 1947 when he was released from imprisonment. He married his wife Charlotte (died in 1988) in 1930 and the couple had three sons, all of whom now deceased. On 29 January 2018, following the death of 113-year-old Francisco Núñez Olivera of Spain, Gerneth became the oldest living man in Europe. On 20 January 2019, following the death of 113-year-old Masazō Nonaka of Japan, Gerneth became a candidate to the title of the world’s oldest man, as well as possibly the last surviving man born in 1905. Gustav Gerneth died in Havelberg, Saxony-Anhalt, Germany, on 21 October 2019 of natural causes, aged 114 years and 6 days, believed to have been the world's oldest man, although Guinness World Records has not verified his case.

Gustavo Adolfo Domínguez Bastida, better known as Bécquer, (Seville, 17 February 1836 – Madrid, 22 December 1870) was a Spanish post-romanticist writer of poetry and short stories. He is considered one of the most important figures in Spanish literature. He adopted the alias of Bécquer as his brother Valeriano Bécquer, a painter, had done earlier. He was associated with the post-romanticism movement and wrote while realism in literature was enjoying success in Spain. He was moderately well known during his life, but it was after his death that most of his works were published. His best known works are the Rhymes and the Legends, usually published together as Rimas y leyendas. These poems and tales are essential to the study of Spanish literature and common reading for high-school students in Spanish-speaking countries. His work approached the traditional poetry and themes in a modern way, and is considered the founder of modern Spanish lyricism.

Gustave Flaubert ( in French; 12 December 1821 – 8 May 1880) was a French writer. He is best known for his novels. Many people consider him one of the most important French writers of the 19th century. He was born in Rouen, in Normandy, and lived most of his life at Croisset, a small place on the river Seine near Rouen. He died there at the age of fifty-eight. His first published novel, Madame Bovary (1857), is his most famous book. It tells the story of a doctor's wife in a small town who is unhappy with her life and dreams of love and luxury. In 1857, the French state took Flaubert to court because it said that the novel offended public morals. Flaubert was found not guilty, and the trial helped to make the book famous. He then wrote Salammbô (1862), a novel about ancient Carthage. L'Éducation sentimentale ("Sentimental Education", 1869) tells the story of a young man in Paris before and during the Revolution of 1848. La Tentation de saint Antoine ("The Temptation of Saint Anthony", 1874) is a long dream-like work written mainly as a dialogue. Trois Contes ("Three Tales", 1877) is a collection of three short stories. His last novel, Bouvard et Pécuchet, was unfinished when he died. It was published in 1881. Flaubert worked very slowly and carefully. He sometimes spent a whole week writing a single page. He searched for what he called le mot juste, the exact word that best fitted each sentence. He also believed that a writer should not directly show personal feelings or opinions in a story. He said that the author should be like God in the universe, "present everywhere and visible nowhere". His careful style and his ideas about writing strongly influenced the modern novel. His work influenced writers such as Guy de Maupassant, Émile Zola, Henry James, Marcel Proust, James Joyce and Franz Kafka. Flaubert's letters are also an important part of his writing. He wrote thousands of them, especially to the poet Louise Colet, who was his lover, and to the novelist George Sand, who became a close friend. In these letters, he often explained his ideas about writing and art. From the age of twenty-two, he also had attacks of an illness that most modern researchers identify as epilepsy. He lived quietly at Croisset for much of his life and gave most of his time to writing. Flaubert's father, Achille-Cléophas Flaubert, was born in 1784 in the Aube region, south-east of Paris. His family had been animal doctors for several generations. He studied medicine in Paris, where he was the best student of his year. He worked under Guillaume Dupuytren, one of the most famous surgeons in France. A surgeon is a doctor who does operations. Dupuytren sent him to the Hôtel-Dieu, the main hospital of Rouen. In 1812, he married Caroline Fleuriot, and in 1818 he became the chief surgeon of the hospital. Dr Flaubert became a well-known and respected doctor. A Paris medical directory of 1826 called him one of the leading doctors in France. He treated poor patients for free. He also had liberal political opinions at a time when the French state and the Catholic Church worked closely together. His son later gave many of his qualities to Dr Larivière, the great doctor who appears near the end of Madame Bovary. Dr Flaubert also became rich. He paid a high tax, which gave him the right to vote at a time when only a small number of Frenchmen could do so. When he died in 1846, he left about 800,000 francs, mostly in land and houses. This property included the house at Croisset. The money later allowed Gustave to live without a job and give all his time to literature. Flaubert's mother, Anne-Justine-Caroline Fleuriot, had a sad childhood. Her mother died when she was born. Her father was a "health officer", a man who practised medicine without being a full doctor. He died when she was nine. She was then brought up by Dr Laumonier, the chief surgeon of the Hôtel-Dieu, and his wife. She was eighteen when she married Dr Flaubert. The couple had six children, but three died very young. Three survived: Achille, born in 1813, who became a doctor like his father; Gustave, born in 1821; and Caroline, born in 1824. Gustave Flaubert was born on 12 December 1821 in his father's apartment at the Hôtel-Dieu in Rouen. The family lived in a wing of the hospital that is now a museum about the Flaubert family and the history of medicine. Patients waited for the doctor downstairs. Upstairs was a billiard room, which Gustave and his sister later turned into a theatre. Above it were the children's rooms. "I was born in a hospital and I lived there for a quarter of a century," he later wrote. Gustave therefore grew up among sick people, dying people and dead bodies. From the family garden, Gustave could see the room where his father cut open dead bodies to teach his students. Gustave and Caroline climbed on a trellis to watch through the windows. Their father sometimes saw them and told them to go away. Many readers think these early experiences help explain two parts of Flaubert's work. One is its sadness. The other is his habit of observing human beings closely and without showing much feeling, almost like a scientist. Gustave was very close to his sister Caroline, who was three years younger. From the age of ten, he wrote and acted in plays with her in the billiard room. Later, when he travelled, he wrote her long and loving letters. His older brother Achille was eight years older and soon left for Paris to study medicine, so the two brothers were never close. His mother taught him to read. The family's servant, Julie, first taught him to love stories. He had two important childhood friends. The first was Ernest Chevalier, whose grandfather lived opposite the hospital and told the boys stories about the adventures of Don Quixote. The second was Alfred Le Poittevin, who was five years older. The two families were very close: Alfred's father was Gustave's godfather, and Gustave's father was Alfred's godfather. Le Poittevin gave Gustave books to read and made him dream about the East. Much later, Flaubert dedicated La Tentation de saint Antoine to the memory of this friend. Gustave wanted to write from a very early age. At the age of nine, he told Ernest Chevalier in a letter that a woman who visited his father always said stupid things and that he would write them down. The critic Jonathan Culler later saw this letter as a sign of Flaubert's future interests. Flaubert collected foolish remarks for the rest of his life, and many of them appeared in his later books. As a boy, he also invented an imaginary character with his friends and his sister. They called him "the Garçon" (the Boy). The Garçon was a loud, vulgar and self-satisfied bourgeois who laughed at everything. The children spoke about him as if he were a real person. Some writers have seen the Garçon as an early version of the pharmacist Homais in Madame Bovary. The theatre in the billiard room lasted about five years, from 1829 to 1834, but Flaubert loved acting all his life. He imitated people so well that his father forbade him to imitate some of them because he thought it affected his son too strongly. "Whatever people say," Flaubert wrote in 1846, "the essence of my nature is the clown." In February 1832, Gustave entered the Collège royal de Rouen, the main school of the city. From May of that year, he was a boarder, which means that he lived at the school. The school was old and famous: the playwright Pierre Corneille had studied there in the 17th century. Only about two per cent of French children went to such schools. Board and lessons cost about 700 francs a year, more than a teacher's yearly salary. Gustave was not a very good pupil at first. He was bored and later remembered the school as a place of dull lessons and long hours of study. However, he read a great deal and began to write. His first stories date from 1835 and 1836. In 1837, a small Rouen magazine printed two of his texts. He wrote horror stories, historical tales and a story called Rêve d'enfer ("Dream of Hell", 1837). In 1838, he wrote Mémoires d'un fou ("Memoirs of a Madman"), which tells the story of his first love in a Romantic style. That love was based on a real experience. During the summer of 1836, at the seaside town of Trouville, Gustave, then fourteen, met Élisa Schlésinger. She was twenty-six years old, beautiful, quiet and religious. She had a baby daughter and lived with the music publisher Maurice Schlésinger. She later married him. Gustave never told her how he felt, and no love affair took place. However, he remembered her all his life. Thirty years later, Élisa became the model for Marie Arnoux, the woman the hero of L'Éducation sentimentale loves without hope. Élisa lived until 1888 and survived Flaubert by eight years. At Trouville, Gustave also met an English family, the Colliers. Their daughters Gertrude and Henriette remained his friends for the rest of his life. In his last year at school, in December 1839, Gustave was expelled. A popular philosophy teacher had been replaced by a man the pupils disliked. Gustave led a protest by the whole class. He wrote a letter to the headmaster which twelve of his classmates signed. They included Louis Bouilhet, who later became his closest friend, and Émile Hamard, who later married his sister. The school expelled Gustave and two other pupils. He prepared for the baccalauréat, the final school examination, alone at home. He passed it in August 1840. His father was pleased and gave him a reward: a long journey from 22 August to 1 November 1840 through the south of France and the island of Corsica. Gustave did not travel alone. His companion was Dr Jules Cloquet, a friend of his father and an easy-going Paris doctor who became an excellent guide for the young man. Gustave loved the Mediterranean, its light and its warmth. He wrote a travel book about the journey, Pyrénées–Corse. In Marseille, on the way home, he spent a night with Eulalie Foucaud, a woman who ran a hotel with her mother. It was his first sexual relationship. He wrote to her for a few months afterwards and used the memory in his story Novembre ("November", 1842). By the age of eighteen, Gustave was a tall and handsome young man with broad shoulders, a deep voice, large gestures and a loud laugh. He did not want a profession, but his father expected him to have one. In November 1841, he registered as a law student in Paris. He hated the subject. He copied textbooks without understanding them and was afraid of becoming a lawyer or a public prosecutor. He preferred to visit the studio of the sculptor James Pradier, where he met artists and writers. In November 1843, he met the great poet Victor Hugo there. In March 1843, he made a new friend, Maxime Du Camp, a rich young man who wanted to become a writer and loved travelling. At the same time, Flaubert began a first novel called L'Éducation sentimentale. It has the same title as his famous novel of 1869, but it is a different work. He passed his first law examination in December 1842, but failed the second one in August 1843. Du Camp, who was present, later wrote that Flaubert's mind was so full of art and poetry that it could not take in the dry rules of law. He failed again at the end of the year. In January 1844, Gustave was returning from Deauville, where his father had bought land. He was driving a small carriage with his brother Achille. Suddenly, he fell to the floor of the carriage as if he had been struck by lightning. For ten minutes, his brother thought he was dead. Achille carried him into a house beside the road and bled him at once. Back in Rouen, doctors bled him again "in three places at once". He had a second attack in February. The treatments of the time were painful and useless. They included a strict diet, no tobacco, repeated bleeding, leeches and orange-flower water. During one bleeding, hot water was poured on his hand to make the blood flow. It burned him badly. The attacks returned from time to time for many years. Du Camp described them: Flaubert became very pale, hurried to lie down, and shook all over. Afterwards, he slept deeply and felt stiff and sore for several days. Doctors today generally think that he had a form of epilepsy. Philippe Hecketsweiler, a doctor who studied Flaubert's illnesses in 2022, concluded that the attacks began with strange visions. Some then led to loss of consciousness and violent shaking. Over his life, Flaubert had thousands of attacks, most of them small. His family kept the illness secret. People outside the family learned about it only after his death. The philosopher Jean-Paul Sartre did not believe that Flaubert had epilepsy. In his very long book about Flaubert, L'Idiot de la famille ("The Family Idiot"), he argued that the illness was a nervous crisis. For Sartre, it was the only way in which the young man could escape from the profession that his father wanted for him. Whatever the illness was, its effect was the same. Dr Flaubert gave up the idea of making his son a lawyer. Gustave left law school, went home, and became a writer. Flaubert himself later gave a similar explanation of his illness. If his brain had been stronger, he told Louise Colet, boredom and the law would not have made him ill. In the same year, 1844, his father bought a house at Croisset. The land he had owned at Deauville had been taken by the state for the new railway from Rouen to Le Havre. The house at Croisset was a large 18th-century country house, about four kilometres from Rouen on the right bank of the Seine, in the commune of Canteleu. It had a park, tall trees and a wide view of the river and its sailing boats. The family moved there in June 1844. Flaubert wrote all his major books in this house. In its garden, a path lined with lime trees became what he called his gueuloir, or "shouting place". There he read his sentences aloud at the top of his voice to test how they sounded. People on passing boats were sometimes surprised to hear him. On 3 March 1845, Caroline married Émile Hamard. Gustave felt that he was losing her. When Ernest Chevalier asked what he thought of the marriage, he answered with only two letters: "AH!" The young couple went to Italy and Switzerland for their honeymoon, and the whole family went with them. Gustave disliked travelling in a group, but the journey gave him one of the most important experiences of his life. In Genoa, in the Balbi palace, he saw a painting of The Temptation of Saint Anthony attributed to Pieter Brueghel the Younger. The picture shows the old hermit surrounded by monsters and strange visions. Flaubert could not forget it. During the next thirty years, he wrote three versions of a book on the same subject. Then came a year of disasters. In January 1846, Dr Flaubert developed a deep abscess in his thigh. His son Achille operated on him, but it was too late. He died of blood poisoning on 15 January. Six days later, Caroline gave birth to a daughter, also called Caroline. Two months later, in March, Caroline Hamard died of childbed fever, an infection that often followed childbirth at that time. She was twenty-one years old. Gustave described her funeral in a letter. The grave was too narrow, and the gravediggers had to force the coffin down with a spade and crowbars. Flaubert now organised the life of the remaining family. He helped his brother Achille obtain their father's position at the hospital. Achille lived in their father's apartment at the Hôtel-Dieu. Gustave and his mother lived at Croisset for most of the year and spent the winter in an apartment in Rouen. They took in the baby Caroline because her father, Hamard, was not able to care for her. For the next twenty-six years, Gustave lived with his mother and helped to raise his niece. He never married. His mother, who had never been very religious, lost her faith after these two deaths. On 28 July 1846, Flaubert went to Pradier's studio in Paris. He wanted the sculptor to make a bust of his dead sister and also wanted to discuss a statue of his father for the city of Rouen. Among the guests in the studio, he saw a beautiful woman with long fair hair. She was the poet Louise Colet, who was thirty-five years old. She had already published several books and had won prizes from the Académie française. She was married to a musician, Hippolyte Colet, and had been the lover of the philosopher Victor Cousin. Paris knew her as "the Muse". The attraction between Flaubert and Colet was immediate. Flaubert visited her the next day, and within a few days they became lovers. He returned to Croisset on 4 August. That night, he wrote her his first letter. This was the beginning of one of the most famous exchanges of love letters in French literature. The new railway between Paris and Rouen made communication very fast. A letter posted in Rouen before eleven in the morning could reach Paris that same afternoon. From the first two years of the affair, 104 of Flaubert's letters survive, but only one of Colet's. He probably burned her letters, or someone destroyed them after his death. The affair was unusual from the beginning. Flaubert loved Louise, and his early letters are full of desire. However, he refused to change his life for her. He stayed at Croisset with his mother and his work. During two years, after their first days together, the lovers met only four times. There were three short meetings in Paris and one day at an inn in Mantes, a town halfway between Paris and Rouen. Louise wanted them to live together. She protested, cried and became angry. He answered that love was not the first thing in his life "but the second". The first was the great work that he hoped to write. In August 1848, the affair ended. Louise came to Rouen in June 1851, soon after Flaubert returned from the East, and the affair began again. This second period lasted until 1855. During these years, Flaubert was writing Madame Bovary. His letters to Louise became a kind of diary of his work and contain many of his ideas about art. He sent her his last letter on 6 March 1855. Louise answered him in another way. In 1859, she published a novel called Lui ("Him"), in which Flaubert appears as a cold and selfish man. The critic Albert Thibaudet later suggested why the affair had lasted for several years. It was made almost entirely of letters. Face to face, he said, Flaubert would not have been able to live with Louise for two months. Two friends were now at the centre of Flaubert's life. The first was Louis Bouilhet, a poet and former schoolmate, who was as poor as Flaubert was rich. He came to Croisset every Sunday, read what Gustave had written, and told him directly what was good and what was bad. Flaubert trusted his judgment more than anyone else's. The second was Maxime Du Camp, his friend from his student years. From May to August 1847, Flaubert and Du Camp walked through Anjou, Brittany and Normandy with bags on their backs. They wrote a travel book together, Par les champs et par les grèves ("Over Fields and Shores"). They took turns: Flaubert wrote one chapter, then Du Camp wrote the next. The book was published only after Flaubert's death. In February 1848, a revolution in Paris drove out King Louis-Philippe and made France a republic. Flaubert was in Paris with Bouilhet and Du Camp and saw some of the fighting himself. Twenty years later, he used these memories in L'Éducation sentimentale. Back at Croisset, he had to serve in the National Guard, the citizens' militia. However, he had little faith in politics. He watched the new Republic and the bloody days of June 1848, when the army defeated a rising of Paris workers, with distance and irony. On 3 April 1848, Alfred Le Poittevin died at the age of thirty-one. Flaubert stayed beside the body for two nights, read Montaigne, and wrapped his friend in his shroud himself. He described these hours in a letter to Du Camp. In May 1848, Flaubert began to write La Tentation de saint Antoine, the book inspired by the painting he had seen in Genoa. He worked on it for sixteen months and finished it on 12 September 1849. It was a very long work, closer to a play than to a novel. The book shows one night of visions. The old hermit Anthony is tempted by the Devil, the Queen of Sheba, the gods of many religions and the sciences. Flaubert believed that it was his masterpiece. He read the whole book aloud to Bouilhet and Du Camp at Croisset. The reading lasted four days. After each part, he asked them: "Well?" They did not want to answer. At the end, they told him what they really thought: the book was a failure. They believed that its strong feelings, endless visions and lack of a clear story hid his real talent. They advised him to choose an ordinary subject from everyday life, in the manner of Balzac. Du Camp later told a famous story. According to him, Bouilhet suggested a piece of local news. A health officer named Delamare, in a village near Rouen, had been ruined by his wife's lovers and debts, and she had poisoned herself. The story is at least partly a legend. Delphine Delamare, the second wife of Eugène Delamare, a health officer at Ry, did die at twenty-six, and her husband died a year later. However, Delamare died only a few months after Flaubert left for the East. The case therefore cannot have been suggested in exactly this form in 1849. What is certain is that Flaubert chose the subject in the summer of 1851. Du Camp's memory of the scene was probably changed by his knowledge of the later novel. Flaubert put the Temptation aside, but he never gave it up. A few weeks later, he left for the East with Du Camp. His mother paid for the journey, a large gift for a son who had never earned any money. The two friends left Croisset on 22 October 1849 and sailed from Marseille in November. They spent eight months in Egypt. They visited Alexandria and Cairo, climbed the Great Pyramid, and sailed up the Nile as far as the second cataract in Nubia. Du Camp took photographs of the temples, among the first photographs ever made in Egypt. Flaubert wrote notes and long letters to Bouilhet and his mother. The best-known episode of the journey took place at Esna on 6 March 1850. A servant led the travellers to the house of Kuchuk Hanem, a famous dancer who also sold sex. The servant was followed by a pet sheep with yellow spots painted on its wool and a black velvet covering on its nose. Kuchuk Hanem danced for them, and Flaubert spent the night with her. He described her in his notes with the same care that he gave to temples and landscapes. He wrote about her clothes, jewels, tattoo, a bad tooth and the bedbugs on the wall. On the journey back down the Nile, he visited her again and felt an "infinite sadness". Louise Colet later told him that the bedbugs disgusted her. He answered that they were the most enchanting detail for him because he wanted some bitterness in everything. The historian Michel Winock has written openly about the sexual side of the journey. The two friends visited many prostitutes, and Flaubert wrote about these visits to Bouilhet in a crude and proud tone that was common among young men of his time. However, Flaubert sometimes preferred simply to observe. In the prostitutes' street at Kena, he walked up and down while women in blue, yellow and red dresses called to him. He was strongly impressed by the scene. He then left without touching any of them because he did not want another experience to change the picture in his mind. From Egypt, the travellers continued to Palestine, Lebanon, Rhodes, Asia Minor and Constantinople. They then travelled to Greece and finally to Italy, where Flaubert's mother joined him. The journey also left him with a lasting illness. In Beirut, in 1850, he caught syphilis, a serious disease passed on during sex. He joked about it in a letter to Bouilhet, but there was no cure at the time. For years afterwards, he took mercury, the usual treatment, which was itself poisonous. He returned to Croisset in June 1851. Francis Steegmuller, who translated the travel notes into English, argued that the journey changed Flaubert. In his view, the Romantic who left for Egypt returned as a Realist ready to write Madame Bovary. Flaubert later became angry with Du Camp, who published his own account of the journey in 1854 without paying much attention to his friend's feelings. Flaubert began Madame Bovary in September 1851, three months after his return. He worked on it for almost five years. His letters to Louise Colet describe this long struggle. He had decided to write the opposite of the Temptation. Instead of a noble and fantastic subject, he chose an ordinary provincial story. Instead of a book filled with the author's own feelings, he wanted a book in which the author could not be seen. In January 1852, he wrote that he wanted to create "a book about nothing". Such a book would depend on nothing outside itself. Its style alone would hold it together. This required a new way of writing. The author would not comment on the story or tell the reader how to judge the characters. Style would have to suggest what earlier novelists had explained directly. "Impersonality is the sign of strength," he wrote. At the same time, he searched for the exact word, removed repetitions and sounds he disliked, and read every page aloud in his gueuloir. The work went very slowly. He sometimes needed a week to write one page and a month to write one chapter. He complained that his characters disgusted him and that the book was a burden that was killing him. The novel was finished in the spring of 1856. Maxime Du Camp was now one of the editors of the Revue de Paris, a literary magazine. The magazine published the novel in six parts, from 1 October to 15 December 1856. The editors were afraid of the government, which closely watched the press under the Second Empire. They cut the scene in which Emma and her lover Léon travel around Rouen in a closed cab. Flaubert protested and demanded that the magazine print a note saying that the cuts were not his. When the editors asked for more cuts before the final part, he asked a lawyer, Jules Sénard, for advice. The magazine printed Flaubert's own note to the reader, saying that the text should be considered as fragments rather than as the complete work. The cuts did not protect the book. The state prosecutor's office decided to act against Flaubert, the manager of the magazine, Laurent-Pichat, and the printer, Pillet. They were accused of offending public and religious morals. The trial took place on 29 January 1857 before a criminal court in Paris, the sixth correctional chamber of the court of the Seine. For his judges, Flaubert prepared a document in which he placed the sentences that had been attacked beside similar passages from great writers of the past. The prosecutor was Ernest Pinard. He summarised the novel and said that a better title would have been "Story of the Adulteries of a Provincial Woman". He called the book "lascivious", meaning full of sexual desire, from beginning to end. What shocked him was not adultery itself but the way the heroine seemed to sing "a hymn to adultery". He admitted that Flaubert had talent and argued that this talent made the book even more dangerous. Six months later, Pinard prosecuted Charles Baudelaire's Les Fleurs du Mal. In that case, he won. Flaubert's lawyer, Jules Sénard, knew the family well. In 1848, he had presided over the National Assembly. He defended Emma Bovary almost as if she were a real person and showed how unhappy her story was. He reminded the court that Flaubert was the son of the respected Dr Flaubert of Rouen. Sénard argued that the novel was moral because it showed the terrible results of Emma's actions. He quoted the poet Lamartine, who had said that Emma's punishment was even too severe for her crime. Flaubert proudly wrote to his brother that the lawyer had "flattened" the prosecution with quotations from religious writers and that the courtroom had been full. The judgment came on 7 February 1857. All three accused men were found not guilty. However, the court strongly criticised Flaubert. Literature, it said, should improve the mind and morals rather than show vice. Flaubert was relieved but angry. He wrote to a reader that his heroine had been "dragged like the lowest lost woman into the dock with the criminals" and that he remained "a suspicious author". He dedicated the book to Sénard. The trial made the novel famous. The publisher Michel Lévy printed it in two volumes in April 1857. He had paid Flaubert only 800 francs for the rights for five years. The first printing sold out quickly, and reprints brought the total to about 30,000 copies. Flaubert soon felt that the publisher had treated him unfairly. Lévy made a large profit, while Flaubert never knew exactly how many copies had been sold. Critics were divided. Sainte-Beuve, the most powerful critic in France, praised the novel in the Moniteur. He saw in it the signs of a new generation: science, observation, maturity, strength and some hardness. Flaubert answered that the book was, for him, "an affair of pure art" and nothing more. In October 1857, Baudelaire wrote an admiring article in L'Artiste. Victor Hugo, writing from exile, told Flaubert that he was one of the leading minds of his generation. Other critics attacked the coldness and "realism" of the book, although Flaubert always rejected that word. An English translation was even prepared under Flaubert's direction by Juliet Herbert, the English governess of his niece. He called it a masterpiece, but it was never published and has disappeared. Flaubert did not rest after Madame Bovary. In September 1857, he began a new novel, which he first called Carthage and later Salammbô. After the dull world of Yonville, he wanted to write about colour, violence and the ancient world, which had interested him since his school days. He wrote that few people would understand how sad a person had to be to try to bring Carthage back to life. He described the book as a desert into which his dislike of modern life had driven him. The subject came from the Greek historian Polybius: the war of the mercenaries against Carthage between 241 and 238 BC. Mercenaries are soldiers who fight for money. After the first war between Carthage and Rome, Carthage did not pay its foreign soldiers, and they rose against the city. Flaubert read hundreds of books about the ancient world. He also wanted to see the places himself. From 16 April to 6 June 1858, he travelled to Tunisia and Algeria and walked over the ruins of Carthage. When he returned home, he threw away everything he had written and began again. The book took four more years. He finished it in April 1862. Michel Lévy paid him 10,000 francs for the book and promised the same amount for his next novel. The publisher allowed newspapers to believe that he had paid 30,000 francs, a very large sum. The Goncourt brothers, two writer friends who kept a famous diary, were shocked by the supposed price. Salammbô was published on 24 November 1862. It was successful with the public and quickly influenced fashion. Flaubert hoped that the Empress Eugénie would wear a Salammbô costume at a court ball, but she was told that it showed too much of the body. At the ball at the Tuileries palace on 9 February 1863, the Countess of Castiglione, who had been the emperor's mistress, appeared dressed as Salammbô instead. The first edition sold out in two months, and a second appeared on 10 January 1863. Critics, however, were divided. Sainte-Beuve wrote three long articles about the book in Le Constitutionnel in December 1862. He respected Flaubert but did not like the novel. He found it cruel, strange and too full of learned detail. Flaubert answered him in a long letter. He was much harsher with Guillaume Froehner, a German archaeologist who worked in Paris. On 31 December 1862, Froehner published an article in the Revue contemporaine listing mistakes that he believed he had found in the novel. He even made fun of the spelling of the heroine's name. Flaubert's reply appeared in L'Opinion nationale on 24 January 1863. He answered every point, gave his sources, and explained that the two "m"s in Salammbô were there on purpose so that the name would be pronounced correctly. His letter was sharp and well informed, and the argument ended in his favour. Other critics repeated some of the ideas used by the prosecutor Pinard. One critic in the Revue des Deux Mondes found the same moral coldness in Salammbô as in Madame Bovary. He described the heroine as suffering from hysteria and as a religious dreamer. In 1855, while finishing Madame Bovary, Flaubert had rented an apartment in Paris on the boulevard du Temple. After Salammbô, he spent more and more of each winter in the capital. People had called him "the hermit of Croisset". Now he dressed in a black suit and white gloves and went to the salon of Princess Mathilde, a cousin of the emperor Napoleon III. He was invited to the Tuileries palace in March 1864 and to the imperial court at Compiègne in November of the same year. Even there, according to Du Camp, he defended Victor Hugo, who was living in exile and was one of the emperor's strongest enemies. On 15 August 1866, Flaubert received the cross of the Légion d'honneur. From the end of 1862, he took part in the "Magny dinners", held every two weeks in a private room of a Paris restaurant. The guests were writers and thinkers, including Sainte-Beuve, Théophile Gautier, Hippolyte Taine, Ernest Renan and the Goncourt brothers. Flaubert came to the second dinner, on 6 December 1862, and attended whenever he was in Paris. The conversation was free and often coarse. In February 1863, the Russian novelist Ivan Turgenev came to a Magny dinner for the first time. He and Flaubert became close friends. Jules de Goncourt called Turgenev a "gentle giant". Turgenev visited Croisset in November 1868. Another important friendship of these years was with George Sand. She was seventeen years older than Flaubert and was famous both for her novels and for her independent way of life. She had praised Salammbô in an article, and they began to write to each other in 1863. She joined the Magny dinners in 1866, the only woman among the men. She stayed at Croisset in April and November of that year and again in 1868. Flaubert called her "dear master" and spent Christmas 1869 at her house at Nohant. Their letters form a long and friendly argument between two very different ideas about life and art. Sand believed in progress, in ordinary people and in the writer's duty to show personal feeling. Flaubert did not share these beliefs. Two women were also important in his private life. Flaubert had raised his niece Caroline almost like a daughter. On 6 April 1864, she married Ernest Commanville, a timber merchant. There was also Juliet Herbert, the English governess who had taught Caroline. Flaubert kept his relationship with her so secret that little is known about it. He visited England in 1866 and 1871, probably to see her. In September 1864, Flaubert began the novel that he called the "moral history of the men of my generation". It tells the story of Frédéric Moreau, a young man from the provinces who comes to Paris in 1840. He falls in love with a married woman, Madame Arnoux, and wastes much of his life in dreams and plans that he never fully carries out. Behind his story, the novel shows French society in the years before and during the Revolution of 1848. Flaubert wanted every detail in the book to be accurate. He read large numbers of newspapers and political books from the 1840s. He questioned George Sand, Du Camp, Maurice Schlésinger and other people who had seen the events of 1848. He also used the history of the revolution written by Marie d'Agoult under the name Daniel Stern. Some sentences in the novel come almost directly from her book. He went to Paris to discover what people could eat at a fashionable café in 1847 and how a funeral was organised. He wrote to Turgenev that he was looking for "the most stupid information one could imagine". He finished the book on 16 May 1869. Two months later, on 18 July, Louis Bouilhet died. He had not been able to read the last two chapters. Flaubert had lost his best friend and his first reader. He gave the manuscript to Du Camp, who checked it for three weeks and found 251 problems of grammar and style. Flaubert accepted most of his suggestions but rejected 87 of them. He argued that style and grammar were two different things and that the main law for a writer was harmony. On 13 October, Sainte-Beuve also died. L'Éducation sentimentale was published by Michel Lévy on 17 November 1869. Most reviews were negative. Critics found the book flat, vulgar and cruel. The Catholic writer Barbey d'Aurevilly accused Flaubert of laughing at every ideal and of suggesting that no heroes were left in the world. The feminist journalist Amélie Bosquet, an old friend, attacked the novel from another direction because it made fun of the women's movement. Only a few friends, such as George Sand and Théodore de Banville, defended the book. Flaubert never understood why it had failed with critics and readers. He was tired, sad and lonely. On 19 July 1870, France declared war on Prussia. The French armies were defeated in a few weeks. On 4 September, the Empire fell and a republic was proclaimed. Flaubert, who had usually shown little interest in politics, became very angry. He said that he wanted "to eat Prussians". He became a lieutenant in the National Guard company of Croisset. He trained his men and went to Rouen to learn how to be a soldier. At the same time, he hid the manuscript of his Temptation of Saint Anthony in the garden. Relatives who were escaping from the war filled the house. In December 1870, Prussian soldiers reached Rouen. In the middle of the month, seven soldiers and three officers were placed at Croisset, together with six horses that had to be fed. Flaubert and his mother left the house and took shelter in Rouen. He wrote to his niece that it was painful to hear the soldiers drag their swords along the path and to have their horses breathe in his face. The Prussians left Croisset after forty-five days, but more came in February 1871. Flaubert stopped wearing the ribbon of the Légion d'honneur because he felt that the words "honour" and "French" no longer went together. In March 1871, the people of Paris rose against the new government and created the Paris Commune. The government defeated it in May with great bloodshed. Flaubert watched these events with horror and despair. He told a friend that he was seeing "the end of the Latin world". From then on, his letters often expressed anger against his time, universal voting rights, the press, the bourgeoisie and crowds. He wrote that he wanted to recognise only "wise men and fools, the innocent and the guilty". On 8 November 1871, Élisa Schlésinger, the love of his youth and now a widow, visited him at Croisset. On 6 April 1872, his mother died. Flaubert was fifty years old. He wrote that she had been the person he loved most. A few months later, he sent Élisa one of his most moving letters. He called her "my old friend, my old tenderness" and invited her to sleep in his mother's room. Of all the people he remembered from his youth, he told her, her face appeared most clearly. Caroline inherited Croisset, but her uncle was allowed to continue living there. On 20 June, two months after his mother's death, he finished the third and final version of La Tentation de saint Antoine. In October, Théophile Gautier died. Flaubert felt that the friends of his youth were disappearing one after another. In 1873, Flaubert changed publishers. Georges Charpentier, a young man who admired his work, became the publisher of his later books. In the same year, Flaubert sent his first letter to the young Guy de Maupassant.

Gustav Leonhardt (born 's-Graveland, Netherlands, 30 May 1928, died Amsterdam, 16 January 2012) was a famous Dutch harpsichordist, organist and conductor who became well known for playing music from historical periods on period instruments. At the beginning of his career the harpsichord was not yet a popular instrument and music from the Renaissance and Baroque periods was usually played in the same way as music from later centuries. Gustav Leonhardt made his audiences aware of what music by Johann Sebastian Bach would have sounded like in Bach's day. Gustav Leonhardt was born into a Dutch, Protestant family who lived in the countryside. His Protestantism was an important part of his life. His father was a wealthy business man. His parents were both very keen amateur musicians. When Gustav was ten they bought a harpsichord. When World War II broke out life was hard in the country and Leonhardt often had to hide under the floorboards so that he was not sent away to slave labour. When he was not hiding he spent a lot of time practising the harpsichord. Gustav Leonhardt studied organ and harpsichord at the Schola Cantorum in Basel. At that time this was the only place in Europe where it was possible to study how to play early music. He went to Vienna to study conducting because his parents thought that being a conductor was a good way to earn a lot of money. However, Gustav was never very keen on conducting and he spent all his time there in the library studying music scores and copying music out. Most of this music had never been published and had not been performed since the time it was composed. In 1952 he became professor of harpischord at the Vienna Hochschule fur Musik. He met Nikolaus Harnoncourt who had similar interests to his. He soon became professor of harpsichord at the Amsterdam Conservatorium and remained there until 1988. He was also organist at the Waalse Kerk, Amsterdam. This church has a very famous historical organ. He became well known for his harpsichord concerts and recordings. He led the Leonhardt Baroque Ensemble with the English counter-tenor Alfred Deller with whom he made one of the first recordings of some Bach cantatas. The ensemble included his wife Marie, as well as Nikolaus Harnoncourt who played the cello. Together with Harnoncourt he conducted and recorded all Bach's cantatas. Leonhardt lived in a big 16th century house facing one of the canals in the centre of Amsterdam. He looked very serious on the concert platform, but he had a sense of humour and occasionally played a bit of ragtime at the end of a recital. Leonhardt died in Amsterdam on 16 January 2012.

Gustav Klimt (14 July 1862 – 6 February 1918) was an Austrian Symbolist painter. He was one of the most prominent members of the Vienna Secession movement. His major works include paintings, mosaics, murals, sketches, and other art objects, some of them which are inspired by Japanese art. Many of them are on display in the Vienna Secession gallery. Klimt's primary subject was the female body, and his works are marked by a frank eroticism — nowhere is this more apparent than in his numerous drawings in pencil (see Mulher sentada, below). Klimt died of influenza in Vienna in 1918. The painting Portrait of Fraulein Lieser, "was last seen in public in 1925", until it was (sold or) auctioned in 2024.

Jean Désiré Gustave Courbet (10 June 1819 – 31 December 1877) was a French painter. He was the leader of the Realist movement in 19th-century French painting. Courbet was prepared to try out new ideas and ways of painting. His paintings made social comment on the world around him. Courbet's paintings were an inspiration to many other painters, particularly the French Impressionists and Post-Impressionists. Edouard Manet, Edgar Degas, Vincent van Gogh and Henri Toulouse-Lautrec were all inspired by Gustave Courbet's paintings of people. His landscape paintings were an inspiration to Claude Monet, Seurat, Cezanne and many other painters. Courbet was born in 1819, and was the son of Régis and Sylvie Oudot Courbet in Ornans, Doubs. Courbet's sisters, Zoé, Zélie and Juliette, were his first models for drawing and painting. When Courbet was twenty he went to Paris in 1839, and worked at the studio of two other painters, Steuben and Hesse. He was not happy there, and wanted to work on his own. He studied the works of many great masters, including Goya, Velazquez and Titian. He painted several self-portraits at this time. He often returned home to Ornans to hunt, fish and find inspiration in the countryside and country life. In 1846–1847 Coubet travelled to the Netherlands and Belgium where he studied the paintings of Rembrandt, Franz Hals and Jan Steen who all painted in the 1600s. The paintings by these artists often showed realistic scenes and portraits of everyday life. They showed ordinary people at the table together, dancing, writing, cooking, working at trades and in businesses and in the fields. There were many pictures of soldiers. Courbet decided that he wanted to paint scenes of ordinary life the way that these artists did. He did not want to paint scenes from literature, history or mythology like most other artists in France at that time.83 Courbet painted a large picture of everday-life at Ornans. The painting, called After Dinner at Ornans, shows four men who have just finished a meal at a little table, which is perhaps in an inn. One man is playing his violin, one man is lighting his pipe. Courbet sits listening, with his head leaning on his hand. A large dog is curled under a chair. Courbet showed the painting at the Salon Exhibition in Paris. It was a great success. It won a Gold Medal and was bought by the French Government.32 Because of the gold medal, Courbet could hang his pictures at the Salon Exhibitions without having them checked by a jury first. This rule was changed in 1857.55 Courbet's work, and the work of Honoré Daumier and Jean-François Millet, became known as Realism. Like the Dutch painters he admired, Courbet often painted in broad, rough brush strokes. He often used dark earthy colours, particularly brown, in his paintings. In 1849 Courbet saw two people working by the roadside, using small hammers to break large rocks into gravel. One was an old man and the other was a young boy. Courbet painted a picture of this scene. He explained it to a friend "It is not often that one meets with so complete an expression of poverty and so, right then and there I got the idea for a painting. I told them to come to my studio the next morning." The picture soon became one of the most famous scenes of the life of poor people that has ever been painted. It was destroyed during World War II in Dresden.31 Courbet's other important painting that was shown at the Salon of 1850 was a scene of life at his village. Beginning in 1849, he painted the funeral of his great-uncle who had died the previous year. Courbet got all the village people who had been at the funeral to come to his studio and pose for him, one by one, until the painting was complete. The painting was very large, 10 by 22 feet (3.1 by 6.6 meters). The famous artist Jacques Louis David had once painted a very large picture in the same way. David's picture was of the Coronation of Napoleon and showed all the people who were present. Some people praised The Funeral at Ornans but other people were very angry about it. They thought that it was wrong to show the burial of an ordinary man in a huge painting, as if he was as important as an emperor. They thought that it was wrong to show the poor people of a village, with their old clothes and dirty boots, as if they were all as important as lords and ladies.4 Some of the critics said that Courbet was deliberately trying to paint ugliness. Many people came to see the picture and liked the new Realist way of painting. Courbet said: "The Burial at Ornans was.... the burial of Romanticism." Courbet became a celebrity. (He became famous and written about in the newspapers- like a film star.) People said he was a genius, a "terrible socialist", and a "savage".8 During the 1850s Courbet painted many other pictures using common folk and friends as his subjects, such as Village Damsels (1852), the Wrestlers (1853), Bathers (1853), The Sleeping Spinner (1853), and The Wheat Sifters (1854). Courbet then painted another huge picture. This painting is called The Artist's Studio and is about seven years in his life as a painter. He shows himself at the centre of the picture, working on a large landscape painting. Behind him is an artists' model, who is naked. All around Courbet are his friends and people from his village. His mother stands to one side of the picture. Another woman is sitting on the floor feeding her baby. A little boy watches the artist, while a white cat plays on the floor. In 1855 Coubet took this picture, with Burial at Ornan and twelve other paintings to be shown in a big international exhibition in Paris called Exposition Universelle. The two biggest paintings and another one were sent away because there was not enough room. Courbet was angry. He had his own building put up, and showed forty of his paintings.52 Many other artists praised Courbet, but some people laughed at him, and the public did not buy very many of his pictures.84 Because of what he had done, younger artists heard about him and admired him. These included James McNeill Whistler in the United States as well as Édouard Manet in France. In 1857 Courbet showed six pictures in the Salon exhibition. One was a hunting scene and one was a picture of two prostitutes lying under a tree on the banks of the River Seine in Paris. Many people came to the exhibition. The hunting scenes were very popular for decorating the halls and dining rooms of large houses.52 For the rest of his life, Courbet painted erotic pictures like the picture of the prostitutes, and also many more hunting scenes. His last erotic painting was called The Origin of the World and was a close-up painting of female genitals. This painting was not shown in a public exhibition until 1988. He also painted many landscapes, which he began by doing outdoor sketches, then made into large paintings in his studio. By the 1870s Courbet was thought of as one of the leading artists in France. The emperor offered to make Courbet a member of the Légion d'honneur which was the highest honour in France, but Courbet refused to accept it. He believed that he belonged to the poor and ordinary people, not to the high and mighty. At this time, there were many political problems in France. Courbet became involved in the political problems. In 1871, he was blamed because a public monument called the Vendôme Column had been demolished. He was put in prison for six months. In 1873, the new government expected him to pay to have the monument restored and put back. He did not have enough money so left France to live in Switzerland. The government decided to make terms so that Courbet could pay for the column in yearly payments of 10,000 francs for 33 years. Courbet died at La Tour-de-Peilz, Switzerland, on 31 December 1877, one day before the first payment was due. He was 58 and died of liver disease, made worse by heavy drinking.

Alexandre Gustave Eiffel (December 15, 1832 – December 27, 1923;, ) was a French structural engineer and architect. He is known for designing the Eiffel Tower. He also designed the armature (supporting framework) for the Statue of Liberty, New York Harbor, United States.

Paul Gustave Doré (; January 6, 1832 – January 23, 1883) was a French artist, engraver, illustrator and sculptor. Most of Doré's work was wood engraving and steel engraving. Doré was born in Strasbourg. His first illustrated story was published at the age of fifteen. As a young man, he began work as a literary illustrator in Paris. He was hired to illustrate scenes from books by Rabelais, Balzac, Milton and Dante. In 1853, Doré was asked to illustrate the works of Lord Byron. British publishers asked him to do more work, including a new illustrated English Bible. Ten years later, he illustrated a French edition of Cervantes's Don Quixote. His images of the knight and Sancho Panza have influenced later readers, artists, and stage and film directors' ideas of how the two characters looked. Doré also illustrated an edition of Edgar Allan Poe's "The Raven" with larger than usual pages. He was paid 30,000 francs by the publisher Harper & Brothers in 1883. Doré's English Bible (1866) was a great success, and in 1867 Doré had a major exhibition of his work in London. The Doré Gallery in Covelant Bond Street opened after the show. In 1869, Blanchard Jerrold suggested that they work together to make a complete portrait of London. Jerrold got the idea from The Microcosm of London produced by Rudolph Ackermann, William Pyne, and Thomas Rowlandson in 1808. Doré signed a five-year contract with the publishers Grant & Co. He had to stay in London for three months each year. He was paid £10,000 a year for the project. The completed book, London: A Pilgrimage, was published in 1872. It had 180 engravings. The book was successful financially and influenced many people. However, many critics at the time disliked it. Some of these critics wrote that Doré paid too much attention to the poverty in parts of London. His later works included Coleridge's Rime of the Ancient Mariner, Milton's Paradise Lost, Tennyson's The Idylls of the King, The Works of Thomas Hood, and The Divine Comedy. His work also appeared in the Illustrated London News. He continued to illustrate books until he died in Paris after a short illness in 1883. He is buried in Père Lachaise Cemetery in Paris.
Gustave Moreau (; 6 April 1826 – 18 April 1898) was a French painter and sculptor. He is one of the most important people of an art movement called Symbolism.

Gustav Metzger (10 April 1926 – 1 March 2017) was a British artist and political activist. He was best known for developing the concept of auto-destructive art (ADA) and the Art Strike. He was also one of the starters of the Destruction in Art Symposium in September 1966. Metzger was born in Nuremberg, Germany. He was the son of Polish Jews. He moved to the United Kingdom in 1939 as a refugee. Metzger died on 1 March 2017 in London, at the age of 90.

Sir Gustav Victor Joseph Nossal [[Order of Australia (born 4 June 1931) is an Austrian-born Australian research biologist. He is famous for his work in the fields of antibody formation and immunological tolerance. Nossal was born in Bad Ischl. He first grew up in the Austrian capital city of Vienna. After the Anschluss (Nazi Germany's annexation of Austria), he and his family moved to Australia. This was because, although not of Jewish faith, his father's grandparents were Jewish. This meant that Nossal was at risk of being sent to concentration camps due his Jewish background. Nossal was baptised, like his father, and is a Roman Catholic. He studied at the University of Sydney. Nossal has written five books and 530 scientific articles on immunology and similar fields. From 1959 to 1961, he was the assistant professor of genetics at Stanford University. He began serving as director of the Walter and Eliza Hall Institute of Medical Research from 1965. At the same time, he was Professor of Medical Biology at the University of Melbourne. He retired from both of these roles in 1996. Nossal was president of the Australian Academy of Science from 1994 to 1998. He was the chairman of the comittee running the World Health Organization's Vaccines and Biologicals Program from 1993 to 2002. He also served as Chairman of the Strategic Advisory Council of the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation Children's Vaccine Program from 1998 to 2003. Nossal is married to Lyn Beatrix (née Dunnicliff). The couple have four children (two sons and two daughters). In 1970, Nossal was made a Commander of the Order of the British Empire. He was knighted for his services to science in 1977. In 1989, he was made a Companion of the Order of Australia. In 1990, he was awarded the Albert Einstein World Award of Science. In 2000, he was named Australian of the Year. Nossal High School in Berwick, Victoria, is named after him.

Gustave Marchegay (25 August 1859 – 19 June 1932) in Bains-les-Bains, is a French architect, watercolourist and sculptor. Emile Gustave Marchegay was born on 25 August 1859 in Saint-Germain-de-Prinçay, in Vendée. Admitted in 1881 to the École Polytechnique, he joins the École nationale supérieure des Beaux-Arts from which he graduated in 1885. Gustave Marchegay then becomes architect of the City of Paris, and will thus be an inspector at the facilities of the Great Exhibition of 1900. As an Engineer of Arts and Manufactures, he was named Knight of the Legion of Honor on August 14, 1900. On behalf of his architectural firm, established rue de Tournon in Paris, he drew up the plans for the châteaux of Coupigny in Orbais-l'Abbaye, and La Bobinière ( Mouchamps, Vendée). We also owe him part of the Célestins barracks and the reconstruction of the buildings of the École alsacienne. As Protestant, he planned the construction of a number of religious buildings in Île-de-France, such as the chapel in Ville-d'Avray. From 1928, Gustave Marchegay exhibited at the Salon d'Automne. He quickly became known for his aquatic sculptures, drawing inspiration from the long hours he dedicated to his passion.: fishing. He died on 19 June 1932 in Bains-les-Bains, and is buried in the Montparnasse Cemetery. Gustave Marchegay married in 1885 the granddaughter of Désiré Nisard, writer member of the French Academy. Some of his sculptures are kept at the Musée d'Orsay, in Paris, as well as at the museums of La Roche-sur-Yon and of Mont-de-Marsan.

Gustave Emmanuel Roy is a (November 13, 1823 in Paris - December 20, 1912 in Paris) was a French merchant of the second half of the 19th century. Son of Auguste Emmanuel Roy, merchant and textile industrialist in Reims, and Annette Carcenac (sister of Henry-Gustave Carcenac), he has a sister, Clara, younger than him. His family has been Protestant for generations. He became an associate of "Carcenac & Roy" in 1847, then of "Gustave Roy & Cie" in 1862. At the head of his company "Roy frères", he became famous. He even became a millionaire, which enabled him, to thank his wife, née Berger, for the birth of her daughter Isabelle, after the infant death of one of the eldest, Hélène, to buy the castle of Faÿ. Elected to the Board of Directors of the Paris Chamber of Commerce and Industry in 1878, he creates the École des hautes études commerciales de Paris (known today as HEC Paris). On December 3, 1881, he inaugurated the school, which then moved to Boulevard Malesherbes. Gustave Roy was also chairman of the board of the insurance company "La France" and a member of the board of directors of the Chemins de fer de l'État, a position in which he campaigned for a revolution in pricing methods. He was also chairman of the board of directors of the newspaper L'Économiste français. He was the owner of Château du Faÿ, located in Andrésy, Château d'Issan and Château Brane-Cantenac with his brother-in-law Casimir Berger. Married to the sister of Georges Berger, he is the father of Gustave Roy (married to Marie Mirabaud) and Ferdinand Roy (married to Hélène Seydoux), as well as the stepfather of Emile Thurneyssen. His second (Hélène) and fifth (Georges) children died at an early age. He is buried in the Père Lachaise Cemetery.

Gustav Vigeland (11 April 1869 – 12 March 1943) was an Norwegian sculptor. He is known for his sculpture in Frogner Park. He designed the Nobel Peace Prize medal. Adolf Gustav Thorsen was born in Halse og Harkmark, which used to be a municipality in Mandal, Norway.

Gustavo Peña Velasco (22 November 1942 – 19 January 2021) was a Mexican football defender and manager. He was born in Talpa de Allende, Mexico. He made 82 appearances for the national football team between 1961 and 1974. Peña died on 19 January 2021, aged 78.

Gustavo Zapoteco Sideño (August 2, 1969 – ), is an Indigenous Mexican poet and writer. He was born in Zitlala, Guerrero. His is Nahuatl people who published modern Nahuatl poems, he's an indigenous activist about arts, culture and speaking regional Nahuatl language from Guerrero Highlands. He started as a poet who wrote many indigenous poems in Guerrero State. Now he lives in Cuernavaca, Morelos State. Cuicatl in yolotl (2002, Ini, Morelos). cuicatl pan tlalliouatlmej, (2004), Conaculta, Morelos. Xóchitl ihuan cuicatl in Morelos (2007, Conaculta, Morelos). Xochitecuan (2012, Conaculta, Morelos). Chalchihuicozcatl (2014, Artes Liberales, University of Warsaw).

Gustavo Gutiérrez Merino (8 June 192822 October 2024) was a Peruvian philosopher, Catholic theologian, and Dominican priest. He was thought to be one of the founders of Latin American liberation theology. He was a professor at the University of Notre Dame. He was known for his writings discussing the question: "How do we [show] the poor that God loves them?". Gutiérrez was born in Lima, Peru. In 2002, Gutiérrez was elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences and in 2003, he received the Príncipe de Asturias award. Gutiérrez died on 22 October 2024 in Lima from pneumonia at the age of 96.

Guy Arnold (6 May 1932 – 4 January 2020) was a British explorer, travel writer, political writer and specialist in north-south relations. He wrote mainly in the areas of African history, politics, and international affairs. He lectured and taught courses on international affairs for over thirty years, at the Workers’ Educational Association and the University of Surrey. Arnold died in London of dementia-related problems on 4 January 2020, aged 87.

Guus Kuijer (; born 1 August 1942) is a Dutch author. He wrote books for children and adults. He is best known for the Madelief series of children's books. He won the Astrid Lindgren Memorial Award from the Swedish Arts Council in 2012. He was one of five finalists for the biennial, international Hans Christian Andersen Award in 2008. Kuijer was born in Amsterdam.

Guy of Dampierre (c. 1226 – 7 March 1305, Compiègne) was the Count of Flanders (1251–1305) and Marquis of Namur (1264–1305). He was a prisoner of the French when his Flemings defeated the latter at the Battle of the Golden Spurs in 1302.

Guus Luijters (3 November 1943 – 3 January 2025) was a Dutch writer and journalist. Luijters started writing in 1972. In 2012 he wrote In Memoriam that is co-written by Aline Pennewaard. The book contains biographies of around 20,000 children who were killed during the German occupation of World War II. The work took seven years to complete. It received national attention after television programm De Wereld Draait Door paid attention to it. An addendum was published in 2013. His 2023 book Verdwenen stad, co-written by Willy Lindwer, also deals with the persecution of Jews during World War II and in particular the role of the public transport operator GVB in Amsterdam in deportations. For his works he received on 7 June 2024 the, awarded by Femke Halsema, who also awarded him with a certificate from Yad Vashem. Luijters was married between 1967 and 1972 with and later married Ruth Visser. He died on 3 January 2025, at the age of 81 years old.

Henri René Albert Guy de Maupassant (; 5 August 1850 – 6 July 1893) was a French writer. He is best known for his short stories. He wrote about three hundred of them in a little more than ten years. He also wrote six novels, three travel books, a book of poems, a few plays, and about two hundred newspaper articles. Maupassant was one of the writers who helped to develop the modern short story, both in France and in other countries. Critics have sometimes seen him as a skilled but simple writer. However, his clear and easy style came from strict training and careful work. Modern studies have shown how much thought and care he put into his writing. Maupassant was born in Normandy, in northern France, and he loved the region all his life. Many of his stories take place there, among farmers, fishermen, and people from small towns. Other stories take place in Paris, where he worked for eight years as a clerk in government offices. A third group of stories is about the Franco-Prussian War of 1870–1871, in which he served as a young soldier. His most famous story, "Boule de suif" ("Ball of Fat"), is about this war. It was published in 1880 and made him famous very quickly. The novelist Gustave Flaubert had been the closest friend of Maupassant's uncle. For about seven years, Flaubert taught the young Maupassant how to write. He taught him to work slowly and to look carefully at the world before writing about it. Flaubert died in May 1880, only a few weeks after the success of "Boule de suif". After this, Maupassant became one of the best-paid writers in France. He wrote for the newspapers Le Gaulois and Gil Blas. His novels Une vie (1883), Bel-Ami (1885), and Pierre et Jean (1888) were very successful. Maupassant's stories are short, clear, and carefully built. They often end with a surprise. They show people through their actions, without long explanations. Many of the stories are sad or cruel because Maupassant had a dark view of human life. He also wrote strange stories about fear and madness, such as "Le Horla" (1887). Maupassant's life was short. He caught syphilis when he was a young man, and the disease slowly damaged his brain. In January 1892, he tried to kill himself. He spent the last eighteen months of his life in a clinic in Paris. He died there in July 1893, at the age of 42. His books are still widely read, especially in schools, and many of his stories have been made into films. Guy de Maupassant was born on 5 August 1850 at the Château de Miromesnil, a large country house near Dieppe, in Normandy. His parents had rented the house in September 1849. The baby was registered under the names Henry René Albert Guy. His father, Gustave de Maupassant, and his mother, Laure Le Poittevin, were both born in 1821. They came from the rich middle class of Normandy. During the French Revolution, the family had quietly stopped using the noble "de" before its name. In 1846, Gustave went to court and won the right to use it again. Gustave was an easy-going man who liked painting and city life. He had little success in business. Laure was an intelligent woman who loved books. Her brother, Alfred Le Poittevin, had been the closest friend of the young Gustave Flaubert. Alfred died in 1848. Because of this old friendship, Flaubert later treated Laure's son almost like a son of his own. Some early biographers even said that Flaubert was Guy's real father. There is no evidence for this story. Guy's younger brother, Hervé, was born in May 1856. From 1859, the family had money problems. Gustave had to take a job in a bank and later in a Paris company that bought and sold shares. About a year later, Laure left her husband. She went to live with her two sons at Étretat, a small fishing village on the Normandy coast. In 1863, the couple were legally separated. Divorce was not legal in France at that time. Laure had money of her own from land and houses, so the boys lived comfortably. Their house at Étretat was called Les Verguies. It had orchards and gardens, and the sea was at the end of the road. Little is known for certain about Maupassant's childhood. Biographers have often said that the separation of his parents hurt him deeply. They point to his story "Garçon, un bock!" ("Waiter, a Beer!"). In the story, a boy of thirteen sees a violent argument between his father and mother, and the experience ruins his whole life. However, this character is very different from Maupassant himself, who was full of energy and enjoyed life. What is certain is that the boy loved the sea, the cliffs, and the free life of the village. He went sailing and climbed the cliffs. From an early age, he liked the company of the sons of fishermen and rope-makers. He joined them in their games and trips. In this way, he learned how the farmers of Normandy spoke. He later used this way of speaking in many of his stories. His mother gave him his first lessons. She loved him but also expected much from him. She often suffered from depression and worried about her health. Marie-Claire Bancquart describes her as an unhappy wife who wanted to keep her two sons close to herself and loved them in an anxious way.
