Maupassant remained closer to his mother than to anyone else for the rest of his life. In 1859–1860, Guy spent a year at the lycée impérial Napoléon in Paris, now the lycée Henri-IV. In 1863, when he was thirteen, he was sent to a Catholic boarding school at Yvetot, a small town between Étretat and Rouen. His mother chose this school even though there was a good state school at Le Havre, twenty miles away. At first, he was a quiet pupil. A letter from May 1864 shows him working for school prizes in Latin, the only foreign language that he ever knew well. In the same letter, he asked for a rowing boat. However, he soon came to hate the school. In a letter to a cousin, he called it a gloomy monastery. He complained about the smell of the priests' clothes, which seemed to him to hang over the whole town. He wrote sad poems about missing home, and his mother kept them. In 1868, the school expelled him. The reason was a poem in which he made fun of the religious life of the school. He never forgave it. In an article of 1885, he described schools of this kind as places of "moral torture". A strong dislike of priests appears many times in his work. One example is the abbé Tolbiac in Une vie. He finished his studies at the lycée of Rouen, the main city of Normandy. There he made an important friend. Louis Bouilhet, a poet and the oldest friend of Flaubert, lived in Rouen. Maupassant later said that, when he was eighteen, he heard a teacher read some lines by Bouilhet during a school walk. He bought a book of Bouilhet's poems that same evening and read almost nothing else for a month. Then he found the courage to knock at the poet's door. Bouilhet read the young man's poems and gave him advice. Through him, Guy also became closer to Flaubert. He had known Flaubert since childhood but had until then approached him only "with timid respect". Bouilhet died on 18 July 1869, nine days before Maupassant passed the baccalauréat, the French school-leaving examination. Flaubert wrote that he had "buried a part of himself". From then on, Flaubert alone guided the young man. Passing the baccalauréat was an important success at that time. Only about two per cent of young men in France received this diploma. During one of these summer holidays at Étretat, Maupassant helped to save the English poet Algernon Charles Swinburne, who had got into trouble while swimming. The grateful poet invited him to lunch. Swinburne and his friend George Powell lived in a small house full of strange objects. One of them was a dried human hand. Maupassant never forgot it. He later used the idea in two stories about a hand that kills, "La Main d'écorché" (1875) and "La Main" (1883). At Étretat, he also met the painter Gustave Courbet. In the autumn of 1869, he went to Paris to study law. He lived in the same building as his father. On 16 July 1870, France declared war on Prussia. Maupassant was almost twenty and was called into the army at once. Because he was an educated young man, he was not sent to a fighting regiment. He passed an examination at Vincennes and was placed in the army supply service, the Intendance, as a clerk with the second division at Rouen. The war went very badly for France. Within six months, the French armies were defeated, the Empire of Napoleon III fell, and the two sides agreed to stop fighting. Maupassant was part of the retreat of the defeated army. He marched for days among tired and disordered soldiers. His feet were bleeding, and he slept outside in the forest of Les Andelys. Once, while carrying orders to the front, he was almost taken prisoner. Rouen surrendered to the Germans without a fight on 6 December 1870. Maupassant was then at Le Havre, which the Germans never occupied. Paris surrendered on 28 January 1871, and the first peace agreement was signed the next month. France lost two provinces to Germany. In the spring of 1871, the workers of Paris rose against the new French government. The government defeated them with great violence. The war was the most important event of Maupassant's youth. It showed him death and destruction on a scale that he would probably never have seen otherwise. After the war, he no longer respected the generals and politicians who had led France to disaster. However, he admired the courage of ordinary people. He used his memories of the war in many stories, among them "Boule de suif", "Mademoiselle Fifi", "Deux amis", "Le Père Milon", "La Mère Sauvage", "Un duel", "Le Lit 29", and "Les Prisonniers". Antonia Fonyi has collected fifteen of his war stories in one volume. In the autumn of 1871, his father paid for another man to take his place in the army, and Guy left military service. Gustave could give his son only 600 francs a year. Like his father, Guy had to find a job. In March 1872, friends with important connections helped him to begin work at the Ministry of the Navy and Colonies in Paris. He was officially appointed in October, but at first he still received no pay. From February 1873, he received 125 francs a month, or 1,500 francs a year. A year later, he was given a regular job. This was about the same pay as a junior clerk or an ordinary worker received. His letters from these years often show his worries about money. He carefully listed his expenses for each month. By the end of 1878, he earned 2,000 francs a year. However, he could not stand the officials above him. In February 1879, after trying for a long time, he moved to the Ministry of Public Instruction. He later said little about his office work. He only said that it was boring and took all his time. However, life in the ministries gave him material for many stories. He wrote about small officials, their routines, and the little men who had power over them. France had about seven hundred thousand minor officials at the time. These were often lonely years. On 6 October 1875, he wrote to his mother that December frightened him. He called it "the black month, the sinister month, the deep month, the midnight of the year". Sport gave him a way to escape. He walked, swam, fenced, hunted and, above all, rowed. On Sundays, he went to villages along the river Seine near Paris: Bezons, Bougival, Chatou, Croissy, and the floating café called La Grenouillère. With four friends, he formed a group of rowers, or canotiers. They shared boats, cheap rooms, and girlfriends, and they enjoyed rough jokes. These friends came from the same middle class as Maupassant. Later, all of them entered respectable careers. With his friend Robert Pinchon, Maupassant also wrote a very rude play, À la feuille de rose, maison turque. The friends performed it privately in 1875 and 1877. Flaubert thought it was very funny. Flaubert did not approve of all Maupassant's way of life. In August 1878, he told his pupil that he was wasting his time rowing and chasing girls on the banks of the Seine. "You were born to write poetry: write it!" he told him. These years of freedom had a terrible result. In a letter to Pinchon dated 2 March 1877, Maupassant said, almost with pride, that he had caught syphilis. At that time, people did not understand how dangerous the disease could become after many years, and there was no cure. It killed at least 30,000 people each year in France. Maupassant was probably treated with mercury around 1876–1877, but this treatment did not remove the infection. For the rest of his life, he suffered from headaches, problems with his eyes, hair loss, and stomach trouble. Later, he began to see things that were not really there. Doctors did not understand these problems, and neither did Maupassant. In one letter from these years, he wrote that his eyes were red and swollen. He said that the fear of becoming blind tortured him all the time. On some days, he added, he felt such horror of life that he wanted to die. From March 1880, his eyes became a serious problem. They grew worse every year and were followed by violent headaches. After 1877, Maupassant never mentioned syphilis again in his letters. During these same years, Maupassant was learning how to write. Flaubert lived for most of the year at Croisset, near Rouen, but spent the winters in Paris. Maupassant visited him there on Sunday afternoons, at his apartment in the rue Murillo. He also sometimes visited Croisset on Saturdays or Sundays. Flaubert read everything that the young man wrote and corrected it. Maupassant later explained their relationship simply. Flaubert, whom he saw from time to time, had "conceived an affection" for him. Maupassant described Flaubert's teaching in 1887, in the essay that opens his novel Pierre et Jean. Flaubert told him that talent, in the words of Chateaubriand, is only "a long patience". A writer, Flaubert said, must look at something for a long time until he sees something in it that nobody else has seen before. Every object, even a fire or a tree in a field, has a part that has not yet been explored. The writer must find this part and describe it with the one right word. Maupassant also said that Flaubert's method was not only to look carefully at things but also to understand what was behind them. Through Flaubert, Maupassant met many of the most important writers of the time. They included Émile Zola, Alphonse Daudet, Edmond de Goncourt, and the Russian novelist Ivan Turgenev, who lived in Paris. Turgenev later helped Maupassant to have his work published in Russia. During one of Flaubert's Sunday meetings in the winter of 1875–1876, the young American writer Henry James met Maupassant. James remembered him telling a fantastic story that could not be repeated in print. Maupassant's first story, "La Main d'écorché" ("The Flayed Hand"), appeared in 1875 under the name Joseph Prunier. For several years, publishers ignored him or paid him very little. Sometimes they did not pay him at all. He signed some of his early work "Guy de Valmont". Valmont was the name of a village in Normandy that some of his ancestors had added to the family name. Under this name, he published a poem called "Au bord de l'eau" ("At the Water's Edge"), which Flaubert had sent to a review. He also wrote a short play in verse, Histoire du vieux temps. It was performed in February 1879 at the Théâtre Déjazet. At the end of the 1870s, Maupassant often visited the house that Zola had bought at Médan, a village on the Seine. Zola had bought it with the money from his novel L'Assommoir. Zola and five younger writers decided to publish a book of stories together about the war of 1870. The other writers were Joris-Karl Huysmans, Henry Céard, Léon Hennique, Paul Alexis, and Maupassant. They called the book Les Soirées de Médan ("The Evenings at Médan"). Maupassant wrote his story in 1879. Its title, "Boule de suif", is the nickname of its heroine, a plump prostitute from Rouen. The name means "ball of fat". Flaubert read the story before it was published. Early in 1880, he wrote to Maupassant that it was a masterpiece, "the work of a master". He said that the idea was original, the story was well built from beginning to end, and the style was excellent. During the same winter, Maupassant had a serious problem. His poem "Au bord de l'eau" had been printed again under the title "Une fille" ("A Girl") in a small review at Étampes, a town near Paris. The local prosecutor, the official who brings people to court, noticed it. Maupassant was threatened with a trial because the poem was considered indecent. He feared that he would lose his job at the ministry. Flaubert, who had himself been tried for Madame Bovary in 1857, wrote a long open letter in Maupassant's defence. Le Gaulois published the letter. The case was dropped. In April, Maupassant's first book, Des vers ("Verses"), was published. He dedicated it to Flaubert. Flaubert wrote that the dedication had made him cry. Les Soirées de Médan appeared on 17 April 1880. Many critics were angry because the book did not show the war in a heroic way. However, almost everyone agreed that "Boule de suif" was by far the best story in the book. At almost thirty years old, Maupassant suddenly became famous. Three weeks later, on Saturday 8 May 1880, he received a telegram. Flaubert had suffered a stroke and was dying. Maupassant hurried to Croisset. He stayed beside the body, and on 11 May he walked at the head of the funeral procession. He later wrote that Flaubert had taken with him "the keenest love I shall ever have for a man". After Flaubert's death, Maupassant asked the ministry for three months of leave with pay. He then asked for more leave with half pay, and finally for leave without pay. He never returned to the office. From June 1880, he earned his living only by writing. From May 1880, Maupassant had a contract with Le Gaulois. He had to write one article or story each week. The contract brought him 6,000 francs a year and lasted until 1888. From December 1881, he also wrote regularly for Gil Blas, sometimes under the name Maufrigneuse. He received similar terms from other newspapers. At the ministry, his salary had been only 2,400 francs a year. Now he earned money quickly. Most of his newspaper pieces were chroniques, essays of about 2,500 words. In them, he gave his opinions on many subjects: politics, science, women, war, hunting, and country life. The stories that he wrote for newspapers were later collected in books. In May 1881, his first collection of stories, La Maison Tellier, was published. The title story is about the women of a small-town brothel. They close the house for one day to go to a first communion in the country. Maupassant told his mother that he thought the story was at least as good as "Boule de suif". The book was dedicated to Turgenev. Turgenev gave a copy to Leo Tolstoy, who did not like it. However, Turgenev then made Tolstoy read Une vie, and Tolstoy became an admirer of Maupassant. Other collections followed quickly: Mademoiselle Fifi (1882), Contes de la bécasse and Clair de lune (1883), and Miss Harriet, Les Sœurs Rondoli, and Yvette (1884). Maupassant also began to travel. He visited Corsica in 1880 and Algeria in 1881 as a reporter for Le Gaulois. His articles about North Africa later became his first travel book, Au soleil ("In the Sun", 1884). He had started his first novel, Une vie ("A Life"), in 1877–1878, with Flaubert's encouragement. He did not finish it until 1883, after many delays and much rewriting. Gil Blas paid him 8,000 francs for the right to publish the novel in parts. He received another 2,000 francs for the Russian translation. The book appeared in April 1883 and sold 25,000 copies within a few months. Hachette, the company that controlled the bookshops in railway stations, refused to sell the novel there because people thought it was improper. Newspapers made fun of the decision. A deputy asked a question about it in Parliament, and Hachette changed its decision. Tolstoy later called Une vie an admirable novel. He said that it was not only Maupassant's best novel but perhaps the best French novel since Victor Hugo's Les Misérables. His new wealth allowed Maupassant to live as he wanted. In 1883, he built a house at Étretat. His neighbour, Hermine Lecomte du Noüy, suggested the name La Guillette, meaning "Guy's house". There he swam far out to sea, walked, and gave parties for summer visitors. He also rented a fine apartment in Paris and, during winter, houses at Cannes on the Mediterranean coast. He could not bear cold weather, and the sun helped his health. In 1883, he employed a Belgian servant, François Tassart, who remained with him until the end of his life. Tassart later wrote a book of memories about Maupassant. By the middle of the 1880s, Maupassant earned about 35,000 francs a year. This was more than ten times his old salary. He worked with strict discipline. He never accepted invitations to lunch because he wanted to keep the whole day for writing. Nobody, not even his father, was allowed into his house in the morning. He refused interviews and, for a long time, did not allow newspapers to publish his photograph. He liked to say that he wrote only for money and that he was a "merchant of prose". Bel-Ami, his second novel, appeared in 1885, first in Gil Blas and then as a book. It tells the story of Georges Duroy, a poor former soldier who becomes rich and powerful in the world of Paris newspapers, mainly through his relationships with women. In the same year, Maupassant travelled through Italy and Sicily with friends. Maupassant never married and never officially recognised any children. In 1903, ten years after his death, a Paris newspaper reported that a woman named Joséphine Litzelmann had had three children by him. They were born in 1883, 1884, and 1887. The biographer Armand Lanoux accepted this story. Christopher Lloyd points out that no proof has survived, so the question is still open. Maupassant now entered the world of rich society. There he became friends with several educated women, such as the countess Potocka and Madame Straus. He kept the details of these friendships very private. One woman, Clémence Brun, known as Clem, worked for him for several years without pay as a secretary when his eyes began to fail. After 1885, Maupassant wrote fewer short works and more long ones. Between 1885 and 1890, he published five novels, two travel books, and nine collections of stories. Mont-Oriol appeared in Gil Blas from December 1886 to February 1887 and then as a book. It is a novel about love and money in a spa town, and it makes fun of the people who visit such places. The collection Le Horla (1887) contains his most famous story of fear. Pierre et Jean, a short novel about two brothers in Le Havre, appeared in La Nouvelle Revue in December 1887 and as a book in January 1888. It begins with the essay "Le Roman" ("The Novel"), in which Maupassant explains his ideas about fiction. Fort comme la mort (1889) and Notre cœur (1890) are novels about love among the rich people of Paris. His second travel book, Sur l'eau ("On the Water", 1888), describes a journey by boat along the Mediterranean coast. It is the most personal of all his books. A third travel book, La Vie errante ("The Wandering Life", 1890), tells about his travels in Italy, Sicily, and North Africa. Edward D. Sullivan has noted that Maupassant's creative power began to weaken after Pierre et Jean. He published relatively little new work in 1888, and much of what appeared in 1888 and 1889 was older material published again. During the summers of 1885 and 1886, he went for treatment at Châtel-Guyon, a spa town in the mountains of the Auvergne. The town later became the setting of Mont-Oriol. He also bought a sailing boat and named it Bel-Ami after his novel. A second, larger yacht, Bel-Ami II, replaced it in 1888. With two sailors as crew, he travelled along the coasts of Provence and Italy. Sur l'eau grew out of these journeys. In February 1887, Maupassant joined other artists and writers in signing a public protest against the building of the Eiffel Tower. He hated the tower. At the beginning of La Vie errante, he wrote that he had left Paris to escape from it. On 8 July 1887, he went up in a balloon called Le Horla, which Captain Jovis had built. The balloon left Paris in the evening. The passengers ate cold chicken and drank champagne while the sun went down. The next morning, the balloon came down at Heist, on the coast of Belgium. Maupassant described the flight in an article called "De Paris à Heyst". His health continued to get worse. His eyes hurt, and sometimes he could not read. He took ether for the pain and employed a secretary who read to him and wrote for him. He saw many doctors and tried treatments at spas and cold showers, but nothing made him better. He travelled constantly. He went to Italy and Tunisia in the autumn of 1889 and to Algeria in the autumn of 1890. Problems in his family added to his own difficulties. His father's bad investments had lost 80,000 francs by 1882. From that time, Guy gave money to both of his parents. His brother Hervé had married and had a daughter, but he could not keep a job. He lived on money from his mother and brother. In 1887, Hervé had already been sent for the first time to an asylum, a hospital for people with serious mental illness. By February 1888, he was behaving violently towards his family. Guy wrote to him that for ten years he had done nothing but suffer because of him and care for him. He said that he was now trying to save Hervé's life. In August 1889, after another violent crisis, Guy had Hervé taken to the asylum at Bron, near Lyon. He wrote to his father that all the money from his new novel would go to Hervé's illness and to their mother. Hervé died there in November 1889. He was 33, had lost his mind, and could no longer move. The family said that he had suffered from sunstroke. In fact, both brothers almost certainly had the same disease, syphilis, which was slowly damaging their brains. In 1891, Maupassant could still work a little. His play Musotte, which he adapted with Jacques Normand from his story "L'Enfant", was performed at the Gymnase theatre in Paris in March 1891. It was a success. That summer, he tried treatments at Luchon, Divonne, and Champel, near Geneva. In December, he wrote his will. He was also trying to write a new novel, L'Angélus, but he never finished it. From the end of 1890, he could no longer write anything longer than short notes. In January 1891, he told his doctor and friend Henri Cazalis: "I assure you that I am losing my mind. I am becoming mad." In December, he wrote to him again: "I am absolutely lost... Death is imminent and I am mad. Farewell, my friend, you will see me no more." During the night of 1 to 2 January 1892, at Cannes, Maupassant cut his throat with a paper knife. His servant François and the sailors of his yacht saved his life. On 7 January 1892, he was taken to Paris and placed in the private clinic of Dr Blanche at Passy. He lived there for eighteen months. The newspapers reported on his illness, and his slow death became something like a public show. His strong body continued to live, but his mind was badly damaged. He could not sleep. He talked without stopping and had strange beliefs. In the spring of 1893, he could sometimes walk in the garden. He pushed small sticks into the ground and said that little Maupassants would grow there the next year. In March 1893, the Comédie-Française performed his play La Paix du ménage. Some people in the audience wondered whether the writer was still alive. In June 1893, Maupassant began to have violent fits. On 28 June, he fell into a coma. He died on 6 July 1893, late in the morning, at the age of 42. The funeral took place on 8 July at the church of Saint-Pierre-de-Chaillot in Paris. Neither his father nor his mother attended. His mother lived at Nice and said that she was too tired to travel. Maupassant had asked to be buried directly in the earth without a coffin. The authorities did not allow this. His body was placed in three coffins, one of pine, one of zinc, and one of oak. Zola, the publisher Paul Ollendorff, and the family's lawyer walked beside the coffin. Maupassant was buried in the Montparnasse Cemetery. Zola spoke at the grave. He said that Maupassant had become famous overnight and that nobody had even argued about his value. People had understood him, Zola said, "because he was clarity, simplicity and strength". Zola ended by saying that Maupassant's work would live. He said that future readers would love him for the song of love that he had sung to life. His parents and his brother's widow argued about what he had left. The yacht and La Guillette were sold. His mother lived for another ten years. She always denied that her sons had died from syphilis. Two unfinished novels, L'Angélus and L'Âme étrangère, were published after Maupassant's death. Maupassant published about three hundred stories in newspapers and reviews. In a complete edition, they fill more than 2,600 pages. Most of them are short, usually no more than 3,000 words, because they had to fit into one issue of a daily newspaper. In the Pléiade edition, only about forty stories are longer than ten pages. A usual story is six or seven pages long, or about 2,000 words. About ten stories are much longer, with more than 8,000 words. These longer stories, called nouvelles in French, are among his best works. "Boule de suif" itself has about 13,000 words. Maupassant put only about seventy per cent of his stories into the fifteen collections published during his lifetime. He left out nearly a hundred stories. Later editors published them again in many different groups. Early critics grouped the stories by subject. There were stories about Normandy farmers, Paris clerks and shopkeepers, war, love, madness, fear, and many other subjects. The index of one complete edition lists 79 themes. Together, they show a dangerous and cruel world: divorce, duels, madness, incest, drunkenness, abandoned women, and murdered children. His characters come from every social class. They include farmers and politicians, rich women and prostitutes, nuns and priests, servants, soldiers and sailors, nobles, criminals, and people with mental illness. A French handbook published in 1992 divides his world into six parts: the provinces, Paris, fear, women, nature, and the "elsewhere" of travel and dreams. Maupassant gave a voice to people whom literature had often ignored. Some of his stories about incest, rape, and abortion can still shock readers. Two worlds appear in most of Maupassant's stories. The first is Normandy, the country of his childhood. Here live the farmers, servants, fishermen, and small landowners of stories such as "Le Papa de Simon", "La Ficelle", "Aux champs", "Le Petit Fût", and "Toine". Maupassant knew their way of life very well. He also wrote their way of speaking with care and affection. "Le Papa de Simon" (1879) tells the story of a boy without a father who finds one in a kind blacksmith. It is the earliest example of Maupassant's mature art. It is a gentle story, written in a style close to that of Alphonse Daudet, but it already shows Maupassant's gift for choosing the right words. The Normandy farmers in his later stories are harder people. They are often greedy, clever in a dishonest way, and cruel. Their tragedies may begin over only a few francs. The second world is Paris. Its characters include small clerks in government ministries, shopkeepers, women who work on the streets, and young men who row on the Seine on Sundays. Maupassant had spent eight years working in a ministry. Stories such as "L'Héritage", "En famille", and "Promenade" show the dull and unfree life of the minor official. Sometimes they also show his quiet courage. His novels are also set in places that he knew well: the country houses of Normandy, the newspapers of Paris, and spa towns. Later, after he became rich, the drawing rooms of Paris society and the villas of the Riviera also entered his work. Maupassant did not invent the modern French short story. Prosper Mérimée had written realistic and violent stories fifty years earlier. The fantastic stories of E. T. A. Hoffmann and Edgar Allan Poe had also been translated into French. Turgenev was perhaps the writer who influenced Maupassant most strongly. From the Russian writer, Maupassant learned how to create a place and a mood with only a few carefully chosen details. He also learned how to show the sadness of ordinary lives. One thing that makes Maupassant different from many writers of his time is his clear story line. His stories are short and easy to follow. They are full of feeling, but the writer usually keeps his distance from the characters. They are modern, but they also continue the old tradition of the tale. The British scholar Trevor Harris has shown how important repetition is in Maupassant's work. The same kinds of people, images, and situations return from one story to another, like reflections in a hall of mirrors. His newspaper articles also help readers to understand his fiction. One of the most striking things about Maupassant's stories is the way they are told. More than 160 of them are presented as stories told aloud, or sometimes written down, by a character. In about half of these stories, a narrator inside the story tells something to a group of listeners: friends after dinner, hunters around a fire, or travellers in a train. This form of storytelling is very old. It can be found in the Decameron and the Thousand and One Nights. It allows Maupassant to keep some distance from the story. It also lets him describe events that he could not have seen himself. Other stories are told through letters or a diary, as in "Le Horla". The critic W. M. Landers wrote that a short story must waste nothing. Everything in it must work towards one main point. In Maupassant's stories, this point is often a crisis, an event that suddenly changes a person's life. The reader often learns the full truth only at the end, and the ending can be a surprise. The critic André Vial compared these endings to the crack of a whip. The most famous example is "La Parure" ("The Necklace", 1884). Mathilde Loisel is the pretty wife of a poor clerk. She borrows a diamond necklace from a rich friend so that she can wear it to a ball. She loses the necklace. Mathilde and her husband buy another one like it and spend ten years working hard to pay for it. At the end, Mathilde learns that the necklace she lost was false. It was worth no more than 500 francs. The story is built so carefully that the cruel ending seems natural rather than a simple trick. Its first sentence recalls Flaubert's Madame Bovary. Like Emma Bovary, Mathilde is a woman destroyed by her dreams of wealth and luxury. Maupassant often leaves the most important things unsaid. The reader must understand them from small clues in the story. He gives no moral lesson and does not spend many pages explaining the feelings of his characters. However, his art is not only about saying little. The Swedish scholar Hans Färnlöf has shown that Maupassant sometimes repeats and develops an idea at length. This makes the reader feel the full importance of one moment in a person's life. In this view, the short story is not simply a small novel. It is a complete telling of one important moment. "Boule de suif" is the story that made Maupassant famous, and it is still his best-known work. The first nine pages describe the French defeat and the German occupation of Rouen. The story shows tired soldiers who look almost like bandits, officers who think too highly of themselves, and townspeople who are eager to please the German soldiers and return to business. Only after this does the main character appear. Ten travellers leave Rouen in a coach for Dieppe. They hope to continue to Le Havre, which the Germans have not occupied. The group has three rich couples, two nuns, a loud democrat named Cornudet, and a prostitute called Boule de suif. Several characters were based partly on real people. Boule de suif herself is often said to have been based on Adrienne Legay, a prostitute from Rouen who really had that nickname and died in 1892. The businessman Carré-Lamadon recalls Pouyer-Quertier, a mayor of Rouen. Parts of Cornudet's character may come from Maupassant's uncle, Charles Cord'homme, who is said to have told him the story. At first, the rich travellers refuse to speak to Boule de suif. Later, when they become hungry, they eat her food. At an inn in Tôtes, on the road to Dieppe, a Prussian officer stops the coach. He says that he will allow the travellers to leave only if Boule de suif spends the night with him. She refuses because she loves her country. The other travellers want to continue their journey. For two days, they put pressure on her until she finally agrees. The next morning, they reject her again. She cries in the coach while Cornudet whistles the Marseillaise. On a first reading, most readers feel pity for Boule de suif and anger towards her false companions. On a second reading, they may notice that Maupassant also shows her faults and gives some real good qualities to the other travellers. The story can also be read as having a wider meaning. It is about war between countries and between social classes. It is also about people who help an occupying army and those who resist it. After 1940, "Boule de suif" became a model for many French stories and films about the German occupation during the Second World War. Another famous war story, "Deux amis" ("Two Friends", 1883), tells of two friends in Paris during the Prussian siege. They go fishing outside the city walls and are shot by the Prussians. The linguist A. J. Greimas, a specialist in the study of signs, wrote a whole book about this story of only a few pages. He studied it sentence by sentence. Two of Maupassant's fifteen collections can show the different kinds of stories that he wrote. Les Sœurs Rondoli was published in July 1884, during the most productive period of his life. It brings together stories first published in newspapers between 1882 and 1884. The book contains many different kinds of stories. There are strange stories about death, such as "Lui ?" and "Suicides", and cruel or comic stories about Normandy, such as "Le Petit Fût". There are comic stories about sex, such as "Les Sœurs Rondoli" and "La Patronne", sharp pictures of society, such as "Mon oncle Sosthène" and "Le Parapluie", and an adventure in a distant country, "Châli". Marie-Claire Bancquart notes that in all these stories Maupassant keeps only the details that are useful. He uses few unnecessary details and little dialogue. Le Rosier de Madame Husson appeared in 1888. The title story takes place at Gisors, a small town in Normandy. A respectable woman wants to reward a pure and good life with a crown of roses and some money. Some villages gave this prize to a "rose girl", or rosière. She cannot find a girl who seems pure enough, so the prize is given to a simple young man named Isidore. He becomes the town's "rose boy", or rosier. Isidore uses the money to get drunk, and after that he never stops drinking. For Louis Forestier, the story makes fun of the awkward and false ways in which people try to appear good. Benjamin Britten later made a comic opera from the story. From 1875 onward, the fear of becoming mad appears again and again in Maupassant's stories. Maupassant believed in science and progress. For two years, he attended the lessons of the doctor Jean-Martin Charcot at the Salpêtrière hospital in Paris. Doctors there studied illnesses of the nervous system. Marie-Claire Bancquart has argued against the old idea that Maupassant's fantastic stories were simply caused by his own illness.

Captain John Guy Dollman BA, FLS (1886-1942) (who was known as Guy Dollman) was a British zoologist and taxonomist. Dollman's Tree Mouse and Dollman's Vlei Rat are named after him. Guy Dollman was the eldest son of the artist John Charles Dollman. He was born on 4 September 1886 and went to St Paul's School. He later went to St John's College Cambridge. In February 1907, when he was still a student, he was employed by the Department of Zoology at the British Museum (Natural History). He spent most of his working life there as Assistant Keeper of Mammals. In 1912, on an expedition to Vietnam, he discovered and named the Tonkin Snub-nosed Langur. He joined the British Army in 1915, and obtained a commission in the 19th London Regiment. He was injured in a bomb accident so he did not fight in the First World War. In 1919, he returned to the museum. He was an adviser to the British group at the 1933 International Conference for the Preservation of the Flora and Fauna of Africa. This was the most important meeting about protecting nature before the Second World War. Dollman helped to decide which animal species needed protecting. He travelled and wrote a lot with Walter Rothschild. Some of their writing included New mammals from Dutch New Guinea (which was published in 1932) and a book about tree kangaroos which was called The Genus Dendrolagus (which was published in 1936). He was also a very good artist, showing pictures at the Royal Academy. He also drew pictures for his own scientific writings. Dollman died on 21 March 1942 when he was 65 years old. Dollman is the binomial authority (the first person to name a species) for the following animals: In 1912, Dollman classified Elephantulus rufescens dundasi, a subspecies of the Rufous Elephant Shrew; In 1912, Dollman classified Rhynchocyon petersi adersi, a subspecies of the Black and Rufous Elephant Shrew; In 1915, Dollman classified Crocidura olivieri zuleika, a subspecies of the African Giant Shrew; In 1932, Rothschild and Dollman also classified Phascolosorex dorsalis brevicaudata, a subspecies of the Narrow-striped Marsupial Shrew. Guy du Merle (1 January 1908 – 6 June 1993) was a French aerospace engineer, pilot and writer. He was the first head of the French Civil Aviation University. Du Merle graduated from the École Polytechnique (1927) and the École nationale supérieure de l'aéronautique et de l'espace (1932). He began his career as a military pilot, from 1933 to 1935, on more than hundred types of aircraft. From 1940 to 1950, he taught aerospace engineering at the École nationale supérieure de l'aéronautique et de l'espace. In 1948, he became the first director of the French Civil Aviation University, until 1951. A roundabout of the city of Toulouse bears his name.

Guy Standing (born 9 February 1948) is a British professor of Development Studies at the School of Oriental and African Studies (SOAS), University of London, and helped start Basic Income Earth Network (BIEN). Standing has written about labour economics, unemployment, basic income and democracy. He wrote the book The Precariat: The New Dangerous Class in 2011. Fellow of the Academy of Social Sciences (FAcSS). Guy Standing's Wikipedia page is interesting because of the photo included. There is an argument about what the caption for the photo should be. The photo shows Guy Standing in a chair, sitting. On the English version of Wikipedia, a user put the title as "Guy Sitting at the 2012 BIEN Congress" to be funny. That was changed to the more correct "Standing at the 2012 BIEN Congress" by another user. Some users would spend time changing it to "Standing Sitting at the 2012 BIEN Congress", while others would change it back, including some Wikipedia Administrators. Both captions are informatively correct, but "Standing Sitting at the 2012 BIEN Congress" was supposedly 'too funny' for Wikipedia. On the English version of the page, the photo featured was changed to one that showed Guy Standing, likely standing.

Guy Ramsay Fieri (,; né Ferry; born January 22, 1968) is an American restaurateur, author, game show host, and an Emmy Award winning television personality. He co-owns three restaurants in California, licenses his name to restaurants in New York City and Las Vegas, Nevada, and is known for hosting many television series on the Food Network. By mid-2010, the Food Network had made Fieri the "face of the network".

Guy Newman Smith (21 November 1939 – 24 December 2020) was an English writer. He wrote pulp fiction-style horror. He also wrote non-fiction, softcore pornography, and children's literature. Smith was born in Hopwas, Staffordshire. He wrote the novel versions of many Disney animated movies. Smith died on December 24, 2020 at the age of 81.

Guy Alexis Herbulot (7 March 1925 – 1 August 2021) was a French Roman Catholic prelate. He was born in Saint-Menges, France. He became a priest in 1950. Herbulot was the Bishop of Évry-Corbeil-Essonnes from 1978 until 2000. Herbulot died on 1 August 2021 in Reims, France, aged 96.

Guy A. Sansaricq (October 6, 1934 – August 21, 2021) was a Haitian-born American prelate of the Roman Catholic Church. He was Auxiliary bishop of the Diocese of Brooklyn, New York from 2006 to 2010. He was born in Jérémie, Haiti. Sansaricq died on August 21, 2021 in New York City, aged 86.

Guy van Grinsven (6 January 1949 Maastricht – 11 October 2021 Maastricht) was a Dutch photographer. Van Grinsven was the founder of "Studiopress" He started his career as an aircraft manufacturer at aircraft manufacturer Fokker. Photography was initially only his hobby, but he already followed a course at the Dutch Photo School. He was employed as a photographer for a period of three years by the National Photo Press Agency, and was Dutch correspondent for the Associated Press. He was also the TV producer and presenter of the weekly program Niveau Bizz Magazine. He was also the publisher of a magazine, Niveau Bizz magazine, which appears in the Euregio Meuse-Rhine. On September 11, 2001, Guy van Grinsven was the only Dutch photographer-cameraman to witness the attack on the World Trade Center in New York. In 2011, Van Grinsven returned to New York to make a new photo series according to the principle of "Dear-Photography" published among others in his own magazine Niveau Bizz Magazine. Since 2012 he has focused on making photo books about cities and their surroundings

Guy Spier (born February 4, 1966) is a Zurich-based investor. He is the author of The Education of a Value Investor. Spier is the manager of the Aquamarine Fund with $350 million in assets. He is well known for bidding US$650,100 with Mohnish Pabrai for a charity lunch with Warren Buffett in 2008. In 2009, he was featured in The Checklist Manifesto, by Atul Gawande regarding his use of checklists as part of his investment process. He is the brother of Tanya de Jager and the grandson of Selmar Spier, the German-Israeli jurist, historian, foreign correspondent and farmer.

Guy Takeo Kawasaki (born August 30, 1954) is an American marketing expert, author, and business person in Silicon Valley. He is famous for his work at Apple, where he helped market the Macintosh computer in 1984. From 2015 to 2016, Kawasaki was on the board of trustees of the Wikimedia Foundation, the group that operates entity of Wikipedia. He has been an adviser of WikiTribune. Kawasaki was born in Honolulu, Hawaii. He went to Stanford University and earned a degree in psychology. He also went to UCLA to get a business degree. He tried law school for a short time but did not like it. Kawasaki is best known for his work as the chief evangelist for Apple. He helped to popularize the Macintosh computer by convincing people to make and use software for it. He used the term "evangelism" to describe this type of marketing. After working at Apple, he started other companies and wrote many books. Some of his books include The Art of the Start and Enchantment. He has also been a well-known public speaker and a member of the board of trustees for the Wikimedia Foundation, until December 2016. Today, he is the chief evangelist for Canva, an online design company.

Guðmundur Þór Kárason (born 14 June 1974) is an Icelandic puppeteer and puppet designer, best known for his work on LazyTown, as well as the voice of Ziggy. He was born in Reykjavík, Iceland. Starting in 2004, Guðmundur was one of the founders of LTS Garðbær Studios (also known as LazyTown Entertainment), puppet performer and voice of Ziggy in LazyTown. In 2010, he was a photographer for the Eurovision Song Contest 2010. In 2011 he was the director and producer for the postcards and made the graphics for the Junior Eurovision Song Contest 2011 in the Armenian capital Yerevan.

Gwendolyn L. "Gwen" Ifill (; September 29, 1955 – November 14, 2016) was an American journalist, television newscaster, and author. She was the moderator and managing editor of Washington Week and co-anchor and co-managing editor, with Judy Woodruff, of PBS NewsHour, both of which air on PBS. Ifill was a political analyst and moderated the 2004 and 2008 American vice-presidential debates. In 2016, she moderate the New Hampshire Democratic Primary debate between Bernie Sanders and Hillary Clinton. She was the author of the best-selling book The Breakthrough: Politics and Race in the Age of Obama. Ifill died of endometrial cancer while under hospice care in Washington, D.C. on November 14, 2016, at age 61.

Gwendolyne Maxine Stacy, also known as Weapon X-31, is a Marvel Comics character created by Steve Ditko. She is Peter Parker's first girlfriend in the comics. In the Ultimate Marvel (Earth-1610) continuity, she becomes Carnage, while in the Ultimate Universe (Earth-6160) continuity, she becomes Mysterio. Bryce Dallas Howard played Stacy in Spider-Man 3, with Emma Stone playing her in both The Amazing Spider-Man and The Amazing Spider-Man 2. Hailee Steinfeld would later voice her in Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse.

Gwen Shamblin Lara (February 18, 1955 – May 29, 2021) was an American author. She is the founder of the Christian diet program The Weigh Down Workshop and of the Remnant Fellowship Church. In her writings, she combines ideas of weight loss programs with those of Christianity. Lara began her diet practice in 1980 because she had weight problems in school. She believed that genetics, metabolism and behavior modification alone couldn't explain why some people were thin and others were overweight. In 1986, Lara founded the Weigh Down Workshop, a weight loss program. Her first book was The Weigh Down Diet. It was first published in March 1997 and has sold more than 1.2 million copies.” On May 29, 2021, Gwen was killed in a plane crash in Smyrna, Tennessee alongside her husband, Joe Lara.

Gwendolyn Midlo Hall (June 27, 1929 – August 29, 2022) was an American historian. She focused on the history of slavery in the Caribbean, Latin America, Louisiana (United States), Africa, and the African Diaspora in the Americas. She wrote Africans in Colonial Louisiana: The Development of Afro-Creole Culture in the Eighteenth Century (1992). Hall died on August 29, 2022 in Guanajuato City, Mexico at the age of 93.

Gwendolyn Elizabeth Brooks (June 7, 1917 – December 3, 2000) was an American poet and writer. She wrote about the ordinary lives of people, often in her own African American community called Bronzeville in Chicago, Illinois. In 1950 she won the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry for her book Annie Allen. She was the first African American winner of that prize. Brooks was born in Topeka, Kansas. When she was still a baby, her parents moved to Chicago. She lived there for the rest of her life. Her father was a janitor. Her mother was a schoolteacher and a pianist. She started writing poetry when she was very young. Her mother told her to send some writing to the well-known poet Langston Hughes. He wrote to her, "You have talent. Keep writing! You'll have a book published one day." Many of her early poems were printed in the Chicago Defender, a newspaper written for African Americans in that city. After winning the Pulitzer Prize for her poetry book Annie Allen in 1950, she wrote a novel called Maud Martha that came out in 1953. This novel tells the story of the main character's life. In the book Maud Martha "suffers prejudice not only from white people but also from lighter-skinned African Americans." From the 1960s on, Brooks' poetry said more about the problems caused by racism in America. Her book In the Mecca spoke about the struggles of Black people to live in their poor neighborhoods. She wrote about the death of Malcolm X. She was active in the Black Power movement. Brooks was named the official poet of the state of Illinois in 1968. In 1985 she was the Consultant in Poetry to the Library of Congress. For these jobs, she went to many places. She went to prisons, hospitals and schools where she asked people to read poetry and to write their poems. She died at her home in Chicago on December 3, 2000. Report from Part One: An Autobiography 1972 The Near-Johannesburg Boy, and Other Poems 1987

Gyalo Thondup, (1928 – 8 February 2025) was the second-eldest brother of the 14th Dalai Lama. He often acted as the Dalai Lama's unofficial ambassador, and was involved in many political controversies around the Tibetan society. In the later years of his life, Thondup repeatedly said that the only way to achieve progress is with China. In 1998, the Central Tibetan Administration (the political arm of the Dalai Lama's anti-China diaspora faction) criticized Thondup for not letting the Dalai Lama know about the CIA's involvement in Tibet. Thondup died at his home in Kalimpong, West Bengal, India, on 8 February 2025, at the age of 97.

Gyan Chand Jain (1923-2007) was an Indian writer and scholar of Urdu literature. Born in 1923 at Seohara of Bijnore district in the Indian state of Uttar Pradesh, Jain was known for his scholarship on Ghalib literature.

Gyaani Shah (15 June 1923 – 8 December 2012), is the first Nepalese woman to join Nepal Army. She is also known for one of the first people in Nepal to promote Christian religion in Nepal after miraculously being saved by a Christian lady.

Paul Nicholas Miller (born August 11, 1988) known by his online username GypsyCrusader, is an American white supremacist. He uses the social media program Telegram to show videos about his political beliefs. He calls himself an investigative journalist and calls his videos "News for Patriots, Christians and God loving Americans." Miller was convicted of making and selling drugs in 2007 and 2009. In 2021, FBI agents and Fort Lauderdale police officers arrested Miller for having an illegal firearm. In Florida, where Miller was, people who have been convicted of large crimes are not allowed to have guns. Miller said he needed a gun because he was afraid of Antifa and Black Lives Matter also claiming it was protection against doxxers. Miller said he did not know he was not allowed to have a gun. The lawyer for the government, Kiran Bhat, said that Miller was dangerous because he was a white supremacist and asked the judge not to let him out on bail before his trial but instead make him stay in jail. Miller's own lawyer said that Miller's videos were only entertainment and theater and that Miller was not dangerous. The judge agreed with that.

Gyo Obata (小圃 暁, February 28, 1923 – March 8, 2022) was an American architect. He co-founded the global architectural firm HOK. He designed the McDonnell Planetarium and GROW Pavilion at the Saint Louis Science Center, the Independence Temple of the Community of Christ church, the National Air and Space Museum and the Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum. Obata died in St. Louis, Missouri, on March 8, 2022, at the age of 99.

Gyula Grosics (4 February 1926 – 13 June 2014) was a Hungarian football goalkeeper. He played 86 times for the Hungarian national football team and was part of the legendary Golden Team of the 1950s. He was nicknamed the Black Panther. He is credited with the paternity of the attitude of an additional defender, for his ability to get out of his own area and for his good attitude to footwork. Regarded as one of the best goalkeepers of all time. Grosics died on 13 June 2014, aged 88.

Gyula Kosice, born Ferdinand Fallik (April 26, 1924 – May 25, 2016), was a Czechoslovakian-born naturalized Argentine sculptor, plastic artist, theoretician and poet. He was of Jewish descent and one of the most important figures in kinetic. He created monumental sculptures, hydrospatial walks, hydrowalls, etc. He made more than 40 personal and 500 collective exhibitions all over the world. Kosice was the first artist to use neon in sculpture and early on water in his work.

György Károly (Károly György, 31 August 1953 – 26 October 2018) was a Hungarian poet and writer. He was born in Budapest. He published his first poems in the weekly Élet és Irodalom (“Life and Literature”) magazine. His best known novels were Folyamatos május and Dunakanyaró. Károly died on 26 October 2018 in Szigetszentmiklós, Hungary from brain cancer, aged 65.

György Baló (14 June 1947 – 18 March 2019) was a Hungarian broadcast journalist and academic lecturer. He was an anchorman for many political talk shows and worked for the Hungarian public television channel Magyar Televízió (MTV) since the 1970s. He was born in Budapest. Baló died on 18 March 2019 from esophageal cancer in Budapest, aged 71.

György Faludy (September 22, 1910 – September 1, 2006), sometimes anglicized as George Faludy, was a Hungarian-born poet, writer and translator. Faludy died on September 1, 2006 in Budapest at the age of 95. He was openly bisexual. 1962: My Happy Days in Hell; reissued 1985,; 2003, 1966: City of Splintered Gods; translated by Flora Papastavrou 1978: East and West: Selected Poems of George Faludy; edited by John Robert Colombo; with a profile of the poet by Barbara Amiel.
